speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the representatives of the governments of France, the United Kingdom and the United States issued a communique last evening after their conference in London. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY FRANCE, UNITED KINGDOM AND UNITED STATES ON SUEZ CANAL
speechtext:
It reads as follows:
The governments of France, the United Kingdom and the United States join in the following statement:
1. They have taken note of the recent action of the government of Egypt whereby it attempts to nationalize and take over the assets and the responsibilities of the Universal Suez Canal Company. This company was organized in Egypt in 1856, under a franchise to build the Suez canal and operate it until 1968.
The Universal Suez Canal Company has always had an international character in terms of its shareholders, directors and operating personnel and
in terms of its responsibility to assure the efficient functioning as an international waterway of the Suez canal. In 1888 all the great powers then principally concerned with the international character of the canal and its free, open and secure use without discrimination joined in the treaty and convention of Constantinople. This provided for the benefit of all the world that the international character of the canal would be perpetuated for all time irrespective of the expiration of the concessions of the Universal Suez Canal Company. Egypt as recently as October, 1954. recognized that the Suez canal is "a waterway economically, commercially and strategically of international importance", and renewed its determination to uphold the convention of 1888.
2.	They do not question the right of Egypt to enjoy and exercise all the powers of a fully sovereign and independent nation, including the generally recognized right under appropriate conditions to nationalize assets not impressed with an international interest which are subject to its political authority. But the present action involves far more than the simple act of nationalization. It involves the arbitrary and unilateral seizure by one nation of an international agency which has the responsibility to maintain and to operate the Suez canal so that all the signatories to, and beneficiaries of, the treaty of 1888, can effectively enjoy the use of an international waterway upon which the economy, commerce and security of much of the world depends. This seizure is the more serious in its implications because it avowedly was made for the purpose of enabling the government of Egypt to make the canal serve the purely national purposes of the Egyptian government rather than the international purpose established by the convention of 1888.
Furthermore, they deplore the fact that as an incident to its seizure the Egyptian government has had recourse to what amounts to a denial of fundamental human rights, by compelling employees of the Suez canal company to continue to work under threat of imprisonment.
3.	They consider that the action taken by the government of Egypt, having regard to ail the attendant circumstances, threatens the freedom and security of the canal as guaranteed by the convention of 1888. This makes it necessary that steps be taken to ensure that the parties to that convention, and all other nations entitled to enjoy its benefits, shall in fact be assured of such benefits.
4.	They consider that steps should be taken to establish operating arrangements under an international system designed to assure the continuity of operation of the canal, as guaranteed by the convention of October 29th, 1888, consistently with legitimate Egyptian interests.
5.	To this end they propose that a conference should promptly be held of parties to the convention and other nations largely concerned with the use of the canal. The invitations to such a conference to be held in London on August 16th, 1956, will be extended by the government of the United Kingdom to the governments named in the annex to this statement. The governments of France and the United States are ready to take part in the conference.

Inquiries of the Ministry
The list annexed to the statement is as follows:
Following Is list of countries to be invited to conference:
Parties to the convention of 1888.
Egypt, France, Italy, Netherlands, Spain, Turkey, United Kingdom, U.S.S.R.
Other nations largely concerned in the use of the canal either through ownership of tonnage or pattern of trade.
Australia, Ceylon, Denmark, Ethiopia, Federal Republic of Germany, Greece, India, Indonesia, Iran, Japan, New Zealand, Norway, Pakistan, Portugal, Sweden, U.S.A.
At the same time I received a personal message from Sir Anthony Eden explaining the real difficulties they have had in settling the list of countries to which invitations should be sent in order to have a basis which would keep the conference within reasonable limits and expressing the assurance that in spite of the fact that within that criteria Canada was not included we would be kept in the closest touch possible during the conference. I can only say that this government supports strongly the objectives of the conference as stated in this communique, and that I am replying to Sir Anthony Eden's personal communication to me that such is the attitude of the Canadian government.

maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN CONNECTION WITH APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have some amendments to suggest with respect to this bill and I had proposed to move them in the usual manner, namely, by moving that the bill be referred back to the committee, but if the government would prefer that I move them on third reading, following the practice in the earlier bill this morning, I would be quite happy to do so.

The purpose of the amendments can be stated quite briefly. They would accomplish the same result as we attempted to accomplish in committee of the whole a day or so ago when the bill was before the committee, namely, to prevent the passage of the proposal to raise the floor on the amount that must be in issue before an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada in a civil case will lie as of right. The proposal now is to raise it from $2,000 to $10,000. We object to that proposal.
The other objection we have is that the government has not provided in the bill that appeals to the Supreme Court of Canada in capital cases shall be as of right. I am not going to restate the arguments with respect to the matter of the increase from $2,000 to $10,000. The objections were quite adequately discussed when the bill was in the committee. But I think I should say a word or two more about the failure to provide that appeals in murder cases shall lie as of right and the government's proposal instead to continue the process of requiring an application for leave to appeal and now providing that that application will be heard by a quorum of five.
One reason why I think this matter requires some further brief discussion is a thoughtful editorial in the Globe and Mail of Wednesday, August 1, which expressed the view that the government's proposal was an adequate safeguard and went as far as was necessary to ensure that those cases of merit would be heard by the Supreme Court of Canada. With respect, I believe that those who hold that view, and of course the minister and the members of the government obviously do, do not quite appreciate the points which are advanced from the other side.
On an application for leave to appeal the full merits of the case will not be automatically before the Supreme Court of Canada and therefore before the judges who hear the application. The application must of necessity involve technical considerations and would properly be opposed on technical grounds. While I imagine that the judges in their character as human beings would be inclined to permit counsel for the applicant to stray somewhat outside the strict field of his application in order that they might hear something about the merits, nevertheless in their capacity as judges of the court they would be properly urged by counsel for the crown to confine the hearing within the narrow limits of the application itself. Therefore it cannot be said with certainty that in every case the hearing of the application for leave to appeal is in effect the same thing as though they were hearing the appeal

itself. If that could be said, then I think there would be the strongest argument along the lines of that advanced in the Globe and Mail editorial and put forward by the minister here that the rights and interests of accused persons are adequately looked after in the government's proposal.
In our view that is not the case for the reasons I have stated, and we feel that nothing short of an automatic right to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada will meet the needs of the situation. With respect to the argument that may be advanced that this would involve a heavy increase in the burden of the court because their time will be taken up by hearing appeals in murder cases, I suggest there is very little difference between the proposal we advance and the government's proposal because I think it is strongly arguable-of course, only experience will prove-that in the great majority if not all cases applications for leave to appeal will be made. Certainly in any case where counsel would have recommended an appeal on the case he will also, if he feels there is any chance of success, apply for leave. You are not going to cut down the number of issues before the Supreme Court of Canada. You will merely alter the form. If our proposal carried, it would be the appeal itself. Under the government's proposal it will be the application for leave. The only difference is that an application will be heard by a quorum of five and the general practice with regard to appeals is that they would be heard by the full court.
I do not think there is going to be very much difference in the burden of extra work that will be put on the court under one process as compared with the other. Personally I do not believe it is a tenable argument that the court would be overworked. I do not believe the court or the minister would advance it but it has been advanced in other quarters, and therefore to meet it I say that there will be very little difference in the number of applications that come before them and very little difference in the amount of work imposed on the court as the result of the fact that an application is heard by a quorum of five instead of by the full court.
A quorum of five means that there are four judges not engaged in hearing an application. As far as other cases are concerned the quorum is never less than three in hearing a case, and I do not think there would be any difference in the amount of work or saving of time or advance in the efficiency of the court simply because you provide that an application shall be heard by five judges. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks):
That the bill be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the
Supreme Court Act
whole with instructions that they have power to amend the said bill as follows:
(a)	by deleting section 2 thereof and renumbering the following sections accordingly;
(b)	by amending present section 19 thereof to provide that appeals from convictions in capital cases shall lie to the Supreme Court of Canada as of right.

speechtext:
Yesterday, Mr. Chairman, the minister spoke at some length in connection with national parks but most of his remarks were of what I would call a general nature and did not, I think, meet the very numerous criticisms which have been made of national parks administration, particularly in western Canada and the province of Alberta where the two largest parks are located. The criticisms which have been made of the way in which parks are administered, of course, are not new. They have been voiced in this committee in I think most years since the war.
First of all, there is the matter of roads. I am glad to hear that there is a program which involves the spending, as the minister has said, of some $60 million over the next eight years in order to improve the roads in the parks. I think that is all to the good. I hope it will be successful in giving us sufficiently good roads in the park that tourist traffic will not be discouraged as has been the case in the past. The road from Banff to Jasper has been a sore point ever since it was first constructed. The road is
now to be rebuilt, I understand, as part of this program and I would hope that a considerable amount of that construction might go ahead this coming year.
Last year and the year before I brought up the matter of better maintenance of these roads. The minister assured me last year that improvement would be made in this regard. However, last year I again heard a very large number of complaints about the condition of that road, so I would take it that there was still not a sufficient number of graders put on that road to keep it in reasonable shape. Another thing I would draw to the minister's attention so far as roads are concerned is that the road in Banff itself, leading immediately into the town of Banff, has been very rough and full of potholes for some years. It seems to me there is no excuse for that particular road especially being left in that condition. I do not know whether any work has been done on it this year, but if none has been done these potholes and the general rough condition of that road should be corrected immediately. It gives an extremely bad impression to the very large number of people coming into Banff to have their car wracked to pieces just on the outskirts of the township and within the town itself. I think there is no doubt that as far as making the parks available to Canadian citizens and citizens from the United States and other places is concerned the provision of good roads is perhaps the most important thing if you are going to get any return business. People come into one of these parks and they strike bad roads in it. It is very unlikely that they are going to come back. Not only do they not come back themselves but they tell all their friends about the bad condition of the roads and thus discourage a _ large number of prospective visitors from coming to the parks.
The next matter in which there has been considerable lagging behind is that of accommodation. There 'is just not enough tourist accommodation in Banff particularly to accommodate the number of people who go there. Many people have to sleep in their cars every night. One of the reasons for the lack of accommodation is the extreme difficulty people have in trying to put up motels, tourist cabins and things of that sort. They have extreme difficulty in getting a piece of land from the park in order to erect tourist accommodation. They run into difficulties of all sorts in trying to erect buildings, once they have secured permission to get the land. Perhaps there may be some fault on both sides as far as this is concerned; but the basic reason there is not more tourist accommodation is the way in which the administration is carried on, the slowness

with which decisions are made and the difficulty people have in trying to do anything along that line in the national parks.
There is also the need for considerably increased facilities of various other kinds. There has been a need for many years for a civic centre and auditorium in Banff. Nothing has ever been done about it although propositions have been put up frequently. There is the necessity there for at least one outdoor movie. There is land available where such a thing could be put up, but permission to construct an outdoor movie has been refused up to date.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes, sir, and it will be.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The situation with regard to people having anything to do to amuse themselves in the evening, particularly in Banff, is very poor. They wander around. Once darkness has fallen they cannot see the scenery. The movie accommodation is extremely limited and very frequently there is really nothing else for people to do.
Another thing which is lacking is ample picnic grounds in the summer time. The picnic ground at Banff is dreadfully overcrowded and many people who want to get into it are unable to find room on the picnic ground. There is also need for improvement as far as hiking trails are concerned. I have spoken about this, I think, for the last 10 or 11 years in this house, the provision of more trails on which people could hike in the summer time and on which they could ski in the winter time.
Another project which a group of people wanted to put into operation was the construction of a gondola lift up Sulphur mountain. We have been refused permission to construct that lift. Why I really do not know. There is a ski lift up Norquay mountain but it is the type of lift which is not very easy for older people particularly to ride up in and many of them are afraid to ride up in it. In view of the fact that a gondola lift up Sulphur mountain would give an opportunity to anybody who comes to Banff, no matter what his general health and physical condition is, to get up on top of the mountain and be able to see the magnificent views which are available from the tops of the mountains, it is very difficult to understand why there has been refusal to construct this lift. There has been consistent refusal to allow this gondola lift to be constructed. I think the excuse that was given was that the road to where the lift would start would not be sufficient to handle the traffic. Well, it seems to me that this is a very poor excuse. To begin with, the road could be improved
Supply-Northern Affairs or widened and I doubt whether there would be any severe difficulty from that point of view, in any event.
I think a whole lot of the difficulties in the national parks come from the fact that you have administration by remote control. In attempting to meet this point yesterday the minister said that decisions have to be taken at Ottawa because they may affect more than one part. I agree that general policy decisions have to be taken at Ottawa. That is quite correct. We should have a general policy which applies to all the parts and I think general policy decisions should be taken at Ottawa, as the minister said. But this is an entirely different matter than every decision being taken at Ottawa as to whether a man is going to build a house or a tourist cabin, or whether he is going to do any little thing at all. As a matter of fact, the same thing should apply as applies in almost every other department, or applies in any business. There should be decentralization. Whilst the general policy is laid down in Ottawa, the local application of that policy should be left to a much greater extent than has been the case before in the hands of the superintendent of the park. The way the thing has been going on, with all decisions having to be taken here in regard to any matter I think involving expenditure of more than $100, it means that the whole business of getting anything done is terrifically slowed down. It is extremely difficult for people to do anything which would help to improve the facilities and the amenities in the park.
As to the situation that prevails there, a letter appeared in the Calgary Herald last November 29, as a matter of fact, written by a man who has been a resident of Banff for the last 51 years. I should like to read some excerpts from it to give the committee an idea of the situation which does prevail. The letter reads:
On your editorial page November 23 you reprint an article from the Camrose Canadian in regard to the tourist attractions at Banff, and having lived there for the past 51 years, I can heartily endorse the criticisms that are made. Once a visitor has taken a dip in the hot springs or the cave and basin, and perhaps taken a ride on the chair lift on Norquay mountain, there is not much left to do, as the small picture theatre cannot accommodate one-tenth of the crowd which lines up for five shows per day.
The parks department in Ottawa has, for many years, adopted a policy to prevent and slow down any improvements or private enterprise whatever.

There is a need for many more attractions at Banff to keep people there, and yet the parks department has refused a permit for the erection of a gondola-enclosed lift up Sulphur mountain from the Upper Hot Springs, making excuses that the road would not be wide enough for the traffic.
Scores of people wish to retire and live in Banff, but cannot get a building site, the government stating that they will only consider applicants who have lived in Banff for 18 months. Yet, they are opening up building lots by the dozen for their own employees or those of the public works department on the trans-Canada highway, and allowing cheap houses to go up which do not meet the requirements they have set for other applicants.
The only major improvements in the Banff park since the war have been two small blocks of building lots put up for tender, with priority to Banff veterans and Banff residents of 25 years or more, and the outsider has no chance to come here to live, yet he is told he may file on a lot after he has been a resident of Banff for 18 months. Where is he to reside during these 18 months?
D. M. Soole.
Mr. Soole is a very well known old-timer in Banff. As stated in his letter, he has been there for 51 years. As a result of all the complaints in connection with Banff the Calgary Herald sent a reporter out there to conduct a thorough investigation of these complaints. Following that, the reporter wrote a series of articles in which he outlined the various things which were wrong so far as he could determine. One of the articles is dated December 12, 1955 and it reads:
There is no vote in this town. What is life like where you have no vote, no say in your municipal government, where your daily affairs are controlled by a bureaucracy thousands of miles away?
In Calgary's own backyard, in the town of Banff, 3,000 persons live under this kind of regime. It is a national park, walled off from the province and run from Ottawa.
There was a series of articles but I do not intend to read all of them. I shall just pick out a few headlines and an occasional interesting excerpt to indicate what is the actual situation. There is no date on this article but it reads:
Remote Control Stifles Growth of Rockies Gem- A. lot of people would call it dictatorship, the way this town is run. Even the more moderate person readily agrees it's a tough place to earn a living, under the iron grip of government control and no appeal against its all-powerful edicts.
This is what the Herald found in an- investigation prompted by recurring and increasing complaints during the past few years of government management of the town of Banff-a federal island inside our province.

I am afraid the articles in the Calgary Herald on which the hon. member bases his criticism have been dictated by commercial interests who are interested in only one thing, in the making of profits out of this great asset

we have in the form of natural grandeur in the west. As I said yesterday, as long as I am in charge of this portfolio there will not be a drive-in theatre in Banff or any other park. You can find those in the cities.
I consider it my duty to see that our national parks are preserved in their natural beauty as much as possible. Visitors will be provided with the essential facilities but not with the ugly things that the commercial interests would like to put up there.
The hon. member referred to the gondola lift. I am sure he is familiar with Sulphur mountain road which leads not only to Sulphur mountain but to the hot springs which are very popular. I do not know whether he has been at the hot springs in the summer and has seen the traffic congestion that creates a hazard on that winding road up to the mountain. I feel that if we had a gondola lift there would be so much more traffic that the hazard would be increased and accidents would be inevitable. There would be traffic jams every day.
We decided that before we asked for tenders for the establishment of a gondola lift we would have to widen the road. I was in Banff in 1954 with my deputy minister and we decided to spend about $25,000 each year in widening and straightening the road. This year we are providing $70,000 so we can finish the road and then be able to call for tenders for the gondola lift.
Then with regard to the picnic grounds. Those grounds may be crowded perhaps on one or two days in the year but they are sufficient. They are being improved constantly. Every year since I have been in the department we have spent large amounts of money improving and expanding the facilities at Tunnel mountain and elsewhere. Last year we spent $50,000 and this year we expect to spend a similar amount. We are always increasing the facilities for the people who want to visit our national parks. We have a limited budget and we must follow strict rules. In spite of what the hon. member for Calgary North has said, and what the Calgary Herald, with the interests behind it, has said, I certainly will not adopt any other course.

Mr. Chairman, I did not plan on getting into this discussion, but I feel the hon. member for Calgary North has indicated a very parochial point of view. I may say that I visited the Alps in Switzerland and Austria before I visited the Canadian Rockies. I think it is important that Canadians should

go to Europe before seeing our own country, because then after having travelled they will see why they have reason to be proud, particularly of our parks at Banff and Jasper.

It is hard to understand why the people of Calgary get so excited about the lack of democracy in Banff where the people do not have the right to elect their civic ruthorities. He tells me that even with the disadvantages that may be considered to exist Banff has the lowest taxes of any place in the west and the fishing is very good.
Mr. Chairman, I hope that the minister will stand by his commitment and will never permit a drive-in theatre in Banff as long as he is minister. I can see a drive-in theatre at Tisdale or a dozen other places on the prairies where they have nothing else to do but to go to these theatres. But to ask the people of Canada and the United States to come to our Rockies in order to see cheap Hollywood pictures in drive-in theatres is I think the last suggestion that should be taken seriously.
The hon. member for Calgary North is complaining because people have to stand in line in order to go to a theatre in Banff. I hope the minister is not going to be influenced by the free enterprisers who would like to make Banff trashy by putting up a lot of cheap theatres to present an artificial picture of life in Hollywood when we have there the most majestic scenery I know of anywhere on this continent. I think the minister is quite right in refusing to yield to those greedy interests in Canada who would like to change Banff into a cheap Coney Island type of place rather than the holiday place it should be for people who want to go to Banff because of the scenery there.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had not planned to take part in this debate. However, my colleague, the hon. member for Bow River because of illness is unable to be here today and, as the minister knows, any discussion concerning Banff national park is something in which he is very keenly interested. He spent a considerable amount of effort and time studying the existing situation in Banff national
Supply-Northern Affairs park, and I am satisfied that many of the arguments advanced so capably this morning by the hon. member for Calgary North would have been supported by the hon. member for Bow River had he been here.
I have visited Banff and I am prepared to admit that it is one of the nicest parks to be found on the North American continent or anywhere else. The scenery is there, the mountains are there, and wild life as well. On the other hand, I think the minister must admit that in order to accommodate the huge tourist traffic visiting Banff during the summer months something more could be done without destroying for one minute the natural beauty that is to be found in the area. I can well remember one word that made an impression on me when I visited Banff the first time. It was as much impressed on my mind when I left Banff as were the mountains, the hot springs and so on. It was the word "occupied".
One evening my wife and I spent hour after hour going up one street ?nd down another trying to find a place to sleep, and we wound up sleeping in the car. Tourist accommodation is not ample in Banff, and I suggest that the minister should give the matter some consideration. Any tourist whc* goes there without sufficient funds to stay at the Banff Springs hotel or the other hotels finds it difficult to get a place to sleep. The minister must know that.
Roads have been mentioned. It is not too long ago that the hon. member for Bow River spoke about the oil on the road leading into the town of Banff. I am very happy to note that the minister has assured us that something is being done to improve that road, and I can only suggest to him that he take in kindly fashion the advice given to him by men such as the hon. member for Bow River and the hon. member for Calgary North. They are not out to destroy the beauty of Banff at all. They are out to make it a better place for all Canadians to visit.
I live close to another national park in the province of Alberta, Elk Island park. We have there the largest remaining buffalo herd, I believe, with the exception of Wood Buffalo park in northern Alberta, to be found in the world. It is a fine park. It has not been destroyed at all by modem buildings. People go there by the thousand to visit the park and to see the fine herd of buffalo. It is located along highway 16 running from Winnipeg to Jasper. I have one suggestion to make to the minister. I suggest that he consider or have his officials consider very seriously the building of a buffalo paddock along the highway with a little road

Supply-Northern Affairs leading off the highway so that tourists in a hurry to go on through can stop and see the buffalo.
This came to my mind last winter as I was travelling to Edmonton. I was in a bus and I noticed buffalo in large numbers along the fence. I heard people say that this was the first time they had ever seen buffalo. The buffalo were there because the salt licks had been located along the fence. I suggest again that the minister give consideration to the building of a small buffalo paddock, perhaps near the main entrance to the park, so that tourists travelling through can see a few buffalo anyway living in their natural state. Perhaps it would encourage them to go into the park and see the fine herd there.
Finally, I should like to make this comment with respect to the national parks I have visited in Canada. I have always been treated with courtesy, and I think that by and large the officials of the minister's department administering the parks are doing a fine job to the best of their ability within the confines of the act under which they must operate. I suggest to the minister that during the holiday season, which we hope will be coming soon, he give serious consideration to a thorough overhaul of the National Parks Act and the regulations associated with it so that when we come here next session we will have something definite to consider.

[Mr. Smith (Battle River-Camrose) .1

one considers the amount of reconstruction that is taking place in those parks. The hon. member seems to forget that the construction season is very short in the national parks. The parks are in many cases in the higher mountain regions, in this instance in the Rocky mountains. Snow is found at the very edge of the highways even in mid-summer, and that is the period when the traffic is heaviest. It does not receive the amount of publicity that is accorded to the other two parks where they are sponsored by the two large railway companies. The hon. member for Calgary North has two difficult problems. Because of the roads he finds that no one is returning to the parks. There is one problem respecting the operators of Kootenay park and Yoho park which I feel is sufficiently important to demand the attention of the minister. While it is not something that comes entirely under his jurisdiction, I would hope that he would make representations to the minister of municipalities in the province of British Columbia. Last evening the minister pointed out that an operator in Banff, with an establishment to the value of $13,000, would pay about $225 in taxes. I should say that an operator in Kootenay park would pay approximately the same amount of tax to the federal government for the various services which he receives and for the concession that he has established. However, in addition he must pay

to the province of British Columbia an improvement, school and hospital tax. This the operator in Banff and Jasper parks is not obliged to do.
The operators have no objection to paying school and hospital taxes, but the improvement tax amounts to about 50 per cent of their total tax, so that they are discriminated against in this way. Their establishment is rated by the department and they are allowed to charge a certain rate for their accommodation, and it is identical in both provinces. Yet I am sure that an operator with the $13,000 establishment would pay in the neighbourhood of $500 in addition to the provincial government, so that in all he would be paying some $700 while the operator in the Alberta parks would be paying about $225. I know it is not something on which the minister can take action on his own, but I would ask that he make representations to the appropriate minister in British Columbia.

I should like to say a word or two in connection with the historic sites service of the department. I was wondering whether consideration should not be given soon to acquiring the homes of former prime ministers and eminent Canadian statesmen. Now, I know that this would cause the department to embark on a considerable expenditure, but it occurs to me that it might be worth while to consider now projects of this kind. Canada is growing very fast. We have now a considerable number of historic properties and they are increasing in number. I feel that it would be worth while for our Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources to consider this matter.
In making whatever tours I have made in the United States I have found that the homes of former presidents of the United States have been nearly all kept as museums and are open to the public to visit and to enjoy. Here in Canada as yet we have not begun projects of this kind. For example, in the town where I was born I remember very
[Mr. Harkness.l

clearly the residence of the Meighen family, the parents of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, a former prime minister of Canada. I think it would be wonderful if some day that property could be purchased. It seems a shame that we have a lot of premises like this that have to be obtained through private subscriptions. I think it would be worth while for the government to consider expending money in this way from time to time to acquire properties across Canada and not merely erect monuments around the parliament buildings at Ottawa. I mentioned the Meighen property because I know about it. Although I am a Liberal member, I would be very proud if our government would consider honouring a former Canadian statesman in this way.
Now, at Brantford we have a large property which I believe was the former summer residence of the Hon. George Brown, one of the fathers of confederation. It is one of the largest farms in Canada, but it is a very interesting property. I am just thinking generally, and I do not want to pick out any particular persons. We all know there are houses right across this country that are of historic interest. I believe it is time we began to consider acquiring some of these properties so that the past of Canada will be brought before this generation and kept as something of which we are all proud. I believe that, although it will cost us money, it will be eminently worth while. Every time I have visited the United States and seen these historic properties I have thought, why do we not have something like that in Canada; why do we not preserve the records of the past? I am only bringing this to the attention of the minister now as something about which I have thought and which I should like him to consider some time in the near future.

He says:
Throughout the first six months of 1956 the first Lacombe troop of boy scouts was preparing for

its annual summer camp. Every boy was working hard, individually and in group enterprises, such as the scouts bean supper, and selling confections at the local ball tournament, since the proposed 1956 camp was a very ambitious undertaking comprising an eight day camping tour of Banff and Jasper national parks. On the eve of departure when all was in readiness, the boys received a rather severe jolt:	Word from superintendent
Strong that the school bus, the scouts' proposed means of transportation, would be charged l cent per passenger mile for passage through the park. It was too late now to call off the plans and the tour proceeded in hopes that some means of avoiding: the toll could be arranged at the park gate. This was not the case, however, and the 32 boys, after eliminating all proposed side trips and by robbing funds originally designated for swimming and other group activities, scraped together the 36 dollars required to get them from the Banff to the Jasper park gate.
Now, I should like to urge the minister to take into consideration group activities such as these, particularly as applied to boys and girls groups, the scouts, C.G.I.T. and other youth activities, because it is a very commendable thing when a bunch of boys go out and earn their own money to take these trips. They were forced because of the regulations-I agree that the regulations were such that superintendent Strong had no alternative but to charge them the fee-to use up their money to pay that toll. They denied themselves group activities, swimming and side trips that they wanted. I am sure that these boys take a rather dim view of the regulations. I can understand why the regulations should be made to apply to commercial vehicles because they are taking these groups through the parks and making money. It is only right that they should pay. However, these boys could have borrowed the family car and taken the trip through the park at the regular $2 fee. Rather than do that they earned the money to hire this bus and because of these regulations were denied the right to take the side trips into these scenes of beauty which the minister described the other day. I would urge the minister to give consideration to the exemption from the regulations of such group activities, the boy scouts and other groups, so that they could take advantage of the tours through the parks to see the wonders of these parks without having to pay commercial tolls.

Mr. Chairman, I will try to make my remarks on this item of the estimates as brief as possible. This morning I was very interested in the remarks made 67509-441
Supply-Northern Affairs by the hon. member for Brantford regarding marks and traditions of our national heritage. In any young country such as Canada, if physical marks of historic interest are swept away, we lose a great deal of our national heritage. In a country as it grows, I think hon. members will be prepared to admit, it is items such as these, visible signs of our past history, that build up national pride and national character. In this respect we have a building in my constituency which I think should be preserved, namely, the city hall of Woodstock, Ontario.
The city hall was granted a plaque by the historic sites and monuments board about a year ago. Only last night the city council of Woodstock approved a motion to allow the plaque, which was granted by the historic sites and monument board, to be placed on the city hall this coming fall. You may ask, why should the Woodstock city hall be singled out by this board for this honour? Well, the reason is this. The Woodstock city hall is the only city hall in Ontario which has been continuously in use as a city hall since it was built. Perhaps I should say it is the oldest city hall which has been continuously in use as a city hall since its construction, which was in 1853. It has served as a city hall ever since that date.
It is interesting to know, Mr. Chairman, that when Upper and Lower Canada were combined the Baldwin act was passed in 1849, and the Baldwin act was the basis for municipal government in this country. It set up municipalities and gave them powers of self-government, and so on. We believe the Woodstock city hall-we have not completely verified it yet-was the first city hall built after the passage of the Baldwin act and, as I mentioned before, it still serves as a city hall and has served continuously as such since that date. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, you might say that Woodstock city hall is the original forum of democracy on the local level as we know it, in what was the original nucleus of Canada, namely, Upper and Lower Canada.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say I think you will agree-I hope the minister will-that this building should be preserved. There has been some discussion at the local level, I know, of building a new city hall because obviously when it was built Woodstock was very much smaller than it is now, and the present building has become inadequate to serve the purposes of a city hall at the present time. There has been some talk of possibly tearing down the building. A great many of us in the area are very upset about this and wish to preserve it. It has been mentioned many

Supply-Northern Affairs times in the house, Mr. Chairman, that municipalities-maybe the federal government is at fault; possibly the provincial government is at fault, I do not know-are pretty hard up for money these days. When you have a valuable piece of property in the middle of a city, while the city may wish to retain a valuable historic building like this, for financial reasons it may not be able to do so. I would certainly hope that the minister might consider, not this year, of course, but next year, placing in his estimates an amount to purchase this building and thus preserve for posterity what was the original seat of local government in a physical sense in Canada. It would be a great shame if this building were to be lost.
There is another matter that I should like to mention very briefly. It is a subject that I have brought up in the house numerous times before; therefore, 1 shall make my remarks on it very brief, as I have already placed on record the pertinent facts about this place. I refer to Long Point island in lake Erie. Hon. members may recall that this island was purchased in 1866, one year before confederation, by a company composed of quite well-off United States citizens, who have since used it as a hunting preserve. The island is in the middle of lake Erie. It stretches out from the Canadian shore. It is 19 miles long and is composed of approximately 19,000 acres. In my opinion this island should certainly be acquired as a national park for the following reasons. Firstly, it has about the finest sandy beach anywhere in the country. Secondly, the water for bathing and swimming purposes off this island is always warm. The reason is, of course, that lake Erie, unlike some of the other lakes and certainly the ocean, being very shallow, never gets very cold. It is an ideal place to bathe in. Since it is very shallow the area is safe for children and people who do not swim very well. More than that, the population of southern Ontario is increasing by leaps and bounds. As hon. members know, it has become a highly industrialized and specialized agricultural part of the country. With the increasing rise in the standard of living and the increase in leisure time, people must have some place to go to spend their vacations and leisure time. While there are many fine beaches on lake Huron and lake Erie, most of them are pretty well taken up. Here we have this island situated within driving distance of an hour or so of London, St. Thomas, Woodstock, Stratford, Galt, Guelph, Brantford, Kitchener and Hamilton, and a thickly populated rural area around. This island is denied to Canadians. It is owned by very few people, most of them from New York.

One or two Canadians belong to this company, called the Long Point Company, that owns this island. They keep private police on the island and do not allow anybody to get on it at all. They use hardly any of the territory. They come there, I understand, only about 10 days in the fall to do some duck shooting. That is all the use they ever make of it.
I am not suggesting that this company, which has kept the island in a fine state of preservation for 90-odd years, should lose all its rights and privileges. I am not suggesting that for a minute. That is not fair. But I am suggesting that the minister make some arrangements with Ontario to acquire a large portion of this island so that the Canadian people may make proper use of it for vacation and recreation purposes. It could be kept as a national park and the wild life be preserved.
I may say that the island is considered one of the best bass-fishing and duck-shooting places in the country. When the bass fishing season opened on last July 1, 25,000 bass were taken in a day adjacent to the island. In addition to this, as I say, this island ought to be made a public place. With the proper restrictions, wild life and game could be looked after. At the present time this island is covered with bush and, as I mentioned, gamekeepers are employed by this Long Point Company. In spite of their looking after it, people do land on the island, and about a year or so ago a large portion of the island was burnt over and some of the original timber was lost forever. If the island were taken over as a national park the timber would be preserved.
I hope that the minister may find it possible to come and have a look at the island. I cannot invite him; I am not one of the exclusive set who own the island, but they would probably let the minister come and look at it. It would not look like Banff national park, which we heard so much about this morning. It would not have mountain peaks. However, I am told that more snakes exist per square yard on the island than in any other place in the world. I am told that there are about 30 varieties and some of them are quite big, about seven feet long. The minister need not be alarmed. I am told that some of these snakes get quite friendly. I remember hearing a story about a young man who was trespassing on the island one evening and sleeping in a sleeping bag. He woke up in the morning and found one of these seven-foot snakes sleeping in the bag with him so I promise the minister that if he should visit the island he will not be in danger.

Then, as I said, duck shooting is still very plentiful. If it was a national park with possibly restricted days with a minimum bag it could be open to the public, as Pelee island is, which is a national park at the other end of lake Erie and which is open to the public for pheasant shooting on certain days. They tell me that at Long Point island you do not even have to take a gun in order to get ducks. There are so many ducks there that they fly into the lighthouse at the end of the island and fall to the ground. If you stand there in the evening when the light is on you can simply pick the ducks off the ground after they have flown into the lighthouse. I have mentioned this matter many times before. I am sure the minister is familiar with this problem and therefore I shall conclude my remarks at this point.

Mr. Chairman, anyone who has been outside in the summer sun today will say that this is an appropriate time to be discussing parks with their cooling streams, wading pools, their swings and the lovely drives in and out; it is very refreshing indeed. As the opposition is showing some inclination to speed up the conclusion of the business of the house I shall just speak for about three minutes.
I hope that some day I will have the opportunity of thanking the minister for the establishment of a long overdue park at Fort William. We have an outstanding site there but it is on the Indian reservation. I am referring to Mount McKay.
No doubt the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe has driven over that mountain and looked out over Thunder bay with its beautiful scenery and all its charm. We have a ski jump there that is not second to the ski jump at Calgary. There is beautiful skiing there and splendid ski trails which are second to none in Canada. This beautiful Loch Lomond about 15 miles around supplies the city with water. It is 800 feet up.
I do not think we have any site in Canada to excel Mount McKay. Of course, the difficulty is that the province and the dominion own this mountain and arrangements would have to be made through the department of Indian Affairs. I hope to see the minister out there this year. If he does come out to see us we will introduce him to something which he has not seen anything to excel.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in taking part in this debate I shall be very brief. I spoke about this matter to the minister at noon.
I would like to see a small park near Fenlon Falls in Victoria county in memory of Champlain. The old Champlain trail which runs from Simcoe lake to Balsam lake has 67509-441J
Supply-Northern Affairs been preserved by the province and the road has been preserved along the same trail. In fact, it is still called the Champlain road and it always will be.
Up near Sturgeon lake there is a place known as the Champlain camping ground. The first house built in that part of the country still stands there. The people who owned it for a number of years kept the house in relatively good repair and although it is not in an excellent condition now it could be cheaply fixed up.
I believe a park could be provided there and that it would not run into much money. I think the province and the county could share with the dominion in the cost and it could be done on the basis of a three-way split in some way or other.
I would like to see a small national park provided there in remembrance of Champlain, the first white man to travel in that country. He made more than one visit to the place and this particular spot was always his camping ground.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the item carries I would like to draw the attention of the minister briefly to one aspect of this branch administration with a reference to historic sites. A moment ago the hon. member for Oxford discussed a historic site in his constituency with the minister and I would now like to draw the minister's attention to another historic site which I think is of even greater importance and about which I spoke on another occasion.
The definition of a historic place in the Historic Sites and Monuments Act is as follows:
"Historic place" means a site, building or other place of national historic interest or significance, and includes buildings or structures that are of national interest by reason of age or architectural
design.
I repeat the words:
... of national historic interest or significance.
Then, under section 3 of the act, the minister is given power to preserve these sites by marking them with plaques and under sub-section (e) he can provide for the administration, preservation and maintenance of any historic place that has been acquired, and so on.
I am thinking of a historic site that does not have to be acquired, one which is presently vested in the department, and located at the foot of parliament hill, the old Supreme Court of Canada building. I can imagine no building which more closely falls within this definition of historic interest and significance than the building in which the supreme court of this country was first established.

Supply-Northern Affairs
When I say "first established", I am not overlooking the fact that at one time the court met in the railway committee room in the former House of Commons. It may be if tradition is justified-I presume prime ministers are often confronted with many problems -that the then prime minister had to placate people and it may be that the then chief justice of Canada did not like the then prime minister too well and the then prime minister did not like the chief justice of Canada too well, and it may be that the chief justice was promised if he moved into this old building that shortly afterwards the new supreme court building would be built.
If that is so, so much the better and all the more reason for preserving this building. If tradition is correct and that building was first used by stonecutters who were cutting the stone for the predecessor of this building, and if afterwards it was used by coachmen who kept their hands and their horses warm while waiting for the cabinet ministers of the day, Sir John A. Macdonald and Alexander Mackenzie, whoever the cabinet minister may have been, then this serves to enhance the tradition, because out of that old building has been evolved the Supreme Court of Canada.
What do we find now? Within three minutes' walk of the old supreme court building which first served as a shed and later served to house the supreme court we have the present magnificent supreme court building. What better symbol could there be of the development of this country than the preservation of these two buildings located within a stone's throw of each other?
In our present Prime Minister we have a gentleman who was a former president of the Canadian Bar Association. He knows and appreciates, as does the minister concerned, the value of tradition and of law and what it has done for this country. Out of the principles of law has evolved everything we preserve and value. I think that of all buildings of historic importance this old supreme court building should be preserved, because, to use the old legal and constitutional expression, the warp and woof of our constitutional development is contained within that building. There is not a lawyer from the Atlantic to the Pacific, nor is there anyone interested in the law, who does not value that building and believe that it should be preserved.
As someone once said, writing of another building:
A nation is not built of stone, to be sure, but it is built essentially of memories that have more force than any statute law or public policy. The stone laid by ancient, nameless masons long ago

and inhabited by the men who made Canada contains the nation's most important asset-its myth.
One might substitute for "myth" the word "tradition". This building is now vested in the crown and I was rather shocked to read the other night that one minister announced that it is shortly to be destroyed. Why is it going to be destroyed and what is going to be substituted therefor? A parking lot. It is proposed to replace this cherished building with a parking lot which could perhaps accommodate 20, 30 or 40 automobiles.
On parliament hill we have a statue of Sir Wilfrid Laurier looking down at the great hotel which bears his name, the Chateau Laurier. We also have here a statue of Sir John A. Macdonald looking at the parliament buildings. He contributed so very much to the establishment of our parliamentary system. We are also going to have a statue of Sir Robert Borden, one of Canada's great constitutional lawyers, and if the proposal I have referred to goes through he will be surveying a parking lot. I hardly think that is in keeping with his station in life, particularly since the old supreme court building can be preserved at very little cost. The building may need a little repair but not very much.
Someone may ask, "What can you use it for?" I would reply by asking why the people of the United States preserve so many buildings in that country. They preserve them as part of their tradition and history. In the city of Philadelphia one can see a little brick building located in the centre of the city. One is almost required to take off his shoes and remove his hat as he approaches it because those people value and treasure it as a part of their national tradition, a symbol of their national development.
There are many hon. members here who lay great emphasis on the necessity of our having a Canadian flag, and with them I do not quarrel. They want all the trappings, shall we say, or many of the tangible signs and symbols of our national development to prove we are a nation. We will not become a great nation and preserve that nationhood unless we preserve the traditions of the past, and that can be done in connection with this building down here more than any other building in Canada. The minister has a responsibility to preserve that building. It is true that there may be some conflict with the ideas of the federal district commission and there may be overlapping jurisdiction with other departments, but for five months I sat in on the committee dealing with the affairs of the federal district commission and

I can say that there is no hard and fast rule that the dicta of that commission shall apply and necessarily be binding. Without taking up further time on this matter I simply want to re-emphasize that in my opinion this building should be preserved and it is the responsibility of the minister to preserve it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to support the suggestion of the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings and urge the minister to take appropriate action with regard to this building. It must be the oldest building among the group on Parliament Hill if it was built originally for the stone cutters and carpenters engaged on the other buildings which grace this site.
Not only is it possibly the oldest building on this site, it has a tradition extending back 60 or 70 years as the home of the Supreme Court of Canada. Special interest should be taken in this building and I deplore any suggestion that it be torn down simply to provide parking space.
The building lacks some of the architectural grandeur of the other buildings, but nevertheless the exterior is of the same material. If there was some care taken in fixing up the roof and windows the building would look much better from the outside than it does at the present time. There is some value in keeping that building as it is and restoring it to make it more suitable than at the present time. It may be used for other purposes, but I suggest that it should be restored to its original condition as the old home of the supreme court. At least one portion should be open for those who are interested, as are so many Canadians, in the past history of our country.
In looking over the records of the Supreme Court of Canada I find that in 1890 an article was written in a United States journal by Mr. Robert Cassels about the Supreme Court of Canada. In describing the building itself, he says, and I quote from page 255 of this publication:
The building in which the court meets is at the extreme westerly end of the government grounds. It is built of the beautiful Nepean sandstone, but without architectural ornament of any kind, having been originally erected for use as government workshops, and since altered to suit the temporary requirements of the judges and the court. The accommodation is quite inadequate to the needs of the court, with the exception of court-room, which with its arched roof and fittings of naturai coloured pine and large Gothic windows is bright and cheerful; it is also easily ventilated and heated, and possesses excellent acoustic properties.
And then at page 241 is to be found a picture of the supreme court room which has just been described in those words. There people can see that court room as it was
Supply-Northern Affairs originally set up and used at the time when there were only six judges of the supreme court. In the American Bar Association Journal of 1946 is an article by E. K. Williams, Q.C., now chief justice of the Queen's Bench, in Manitoba. This deals with the move of the supreme court to its new building, and referring to the new building he says in the concluding paragraph:
The building a photograph of which is reproduced on the cover of this issue of the Journal, is a worthy home for the Supreme Court of Canada, but even so the barristers of Canada, who have appeared before that august tribunal in the comfortable and friendly atmosphere of the old court room, with its faded hangings but excellent acoustics, will think, with nostalgic longings, of the glories of the simpler days now gone, of the great judges who presided and the eminent counsel who pleaded before them, and while rejoicing in the new, will still fondly reminisce about the old.
I submit that this building might very well be preserved as a national shrine in order to give due importance to the judicial branch of the government of Canada. A little pamphlet dealing with the Supreme Court of Canada has this to say:
The government of Canada consists of three branches, the legislative which enacts the law, the executive which administers it, and the judicial branch which interprets.
The Supreme Court of Canada represents the judicial branch. I shall conclude by suggesting that consideration be given to the preservation of this building, the restoring of the central portion containing the old court room to the condition in which it was in the early days, and the making of this building an historic site to which many people could come to see the beginnings of the Supreme Court of Canada. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, the contrast between the old and the new buildings will be immediately evident. Here we have a chance to preserve an important historic site in Canada. As it is situated right in the centre of our national capital on Parliament Hill, we would be well advised to take steps to preserve this building and make it another national historic site and museum; emphasizing the development and growth of law in Canada.

speechtext: Before the item carries I .-should like to ask the minister one question. 'The minister knows that we have had some [DOT]discussions and correspondence with respect -to the proposed acquisition of the park at *Grand Pre as a national park. speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources

speechtext:
The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings made a motion for the production of all correspondence with respect to this matter. Since the correspondence was tabled the following events have happened. However, after my conversation with Mr. Savoie, he went back to Moncton and the directors of La Societe Nationale 1 Assomp-tion had a meeting. On June 29, I received


a telegram from the secretary, Mr. Daigle telling me that following my conversation with Mr. Savoie La Societe Nationale l'As-somption had passed a resolution authorizing the transfer to the department. I immediately advised the Dominion Atlantic Railway of such acceptance by La Societe Nationale l'Assomption so that the offer of the D.A.R. would be held open, and two or three days ago I received a letter from the president, I believe, of the D.A.R. telling me that the offer was open.

Canadian wildlife service-
300. Wildlife resources conservation and development, including administration of the Migratory Birds Convention Act, $472,331.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The minister will remember that about two years ago we had a discussion in the house concerning wildlife in the Northwest Territories, and at that time he gave us a report with regard to the muskox and the government reindeer herds. Apparently reindeer are not considered as wild life, but perhaps the minister could deal with that situation at the same time. I raise this matter because five years ago there was a very interesting article in Maclean's magazine by Vilhjalmur Stefansson in which he had this to say:
As far as reindeer are concerned the United States department of agriculture estimated some years ago that Alaska could permanently support about 4 million head without overgrazing. Since Canada has about ten times as much permanent grazing land, I consider that it could support a reindeer industry of 40 million head, which in terms of pounds of meat is equivalent to about 80 million sheep.

The muskox, whose feeding habits are even better suited to the north than the reindeer, could do far better. I estimate that Canada's north could maintain a hundred million muskox, which is the equivalent of 400 million sheep. What such a vast industry would do for Canada, and what such supplies of food might do to assist in other developments of the north such as mining and oil, I leave to your imagination.
In the intervening years there have been great developments in the north, more particularly in the opening up of the D.E.W. line and the mid-Canada line, and I think it would be very helpful if the minister would bring the committee up to date with regard to these two situations involving the muskox and reindeer herds.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
As members of the committee will know, the muskox is a wild animal. I made a report on muskox two years ago when my estimates were before the house, but it is difficult to know what the numbers are. It is believed that the number has increased, but certainly not to a sufficient extent to allow us to do away with the regulation forbidding completely the killing, hunting or molesting of muskox.
As to the reindeer, I have to say that our experience in the last 20 years has not always been very satisfactory, and I have to admit that in the last year it has been very disappointing indeed. We have always had some trouble in making herders out of the Eskimos, who are natural hunters, but with the jobs available at Aklavik and on the D.E.W. line where a good number of Eskimos are employed it has become even more difficult to interest Eskimos in being herders. But that is not the only disappointment. There is worse than that. The original herd of about 2,300 deer 20 years ago has increased to 6,500 this year but the figure of 6,500 is a decrease from last year.
The losses have been heavy this year. The causes of the losses have been straying, predation, poaching, sickness and injury. A disease of the bones has developed which weakens the spine and has caused the loss of a good number of reindeer. We are trying our best to find something that we can add to the diet of the reindeer to prevent that weakness of the bones. Studies are being made to determine the cause of the weakness and, as I said, we are trying to find what supplementary fodder, mineral salt or other thing we can use to prevent the generalization of the disease.
Reindeer herding has not been easy anyway. In Alaska, as the hon. member knows, they have had serious losses. However, I am really confident that our scientists will find what supplementary food or diet has to be given to these animals so that they can continue to grow in numbers. After all, the
Supply-Northern Ayairs meat of these herds is the only meat the people of Aklavik and the Arctic coast and especially the people of the delta of the Mackenzie can get except that when there is a real scarcity we fly in buffalo meat from Wood Buffalo park.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Are they having some trouble in Alaska with the reindeer?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: There are very few. They have declined at a terrific pace. In one year-I do not remember which one-I believe they came close to disappearing completely.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What about caribou herds?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The story is not any more encouraging. This is quite a serious problem for the natives, this depleting of the caribou reserves. According to a survey which was made in 1950, in the Northwest Territories there were approximately 670,000 head of caribou. According to the survey of last year-that is in 1955-the number was approximately 300,000 which is less than half. That decrease occurred in five years. Caribou is a major source of meat for the Indians of the Mackenzie valley and for the Eskimos of the Keewatin district. This decline we consider is most serious. The causes of it appear to be predation, human utilization, forest fires, unfavourable weather and the parasites. Since last year, we had a very good discussion on that subject, or rather I should say that there has been discussion. I was not there. My deputy as commissioner of the Northwest Territories had with the members of the territorial council a very full discussion of what should and could be done in the way of conservation in order to try to increase the herds of caribou and bring them back to the numbers that we used to have. It was felt that we should increase our predator control, something which has been done all over the territories. By the known means of wolf traps and poisoning we have taken a much greater number of wolves this winter than ever in the past and we hope that this control will help somewhat to bring back the herds of caribou to what they were.
Another thing that we have done is steadily to increase our educational program among the natives with respect to conservation. I have here in my hand a booklet which is written in Eskimo and which has been widely distributed. It teaches the Eskimos in a simple manner the rules of conservation and what they should do. It tells them not to kill more than they need, and not to leave any meat around as they used to do in the past when the caribou were plentiful. We are really doing our best. By all known

Supply-Northern Affairs means we have sought to teach the Indians and the Eskimos the rules of conservation in the case of caribou.
Finally, in the north and here in Ottawa we have formed technical and administrative committees. We have formed those committees with representatives of the federal and provincial governments, because some of the caribou come down below the 60th parallel into Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. The provincial governments have been very co-operative. At this time I wish to express my appreciation of that co-operation. In a few words I would sum up the situation in this way. As far as reindeer are concerned, the situation is disappointing. As far as caribou are concerned, it is more than disappointing. But, with the measures we are taking, we hope that we can overcome these difficulties and bring the herds back to what they were.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The minister said there now were about 6,500 reindeer?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: About 6,500.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The figure on December 10, 1953, was 7,730.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I understand this service functions somewhat in the backwaters of the department's activities, at least so far as the public is concerned. Wildlife is a very important thing to consider in any development in this country, whether of water resources, forest resources or of park areas. What I am wondering is this. Is it the practice of the minister to have the senior officials of the wildlife service present when a conference is being held to make decisions with respect to any forest development or water development in this country? I think it is a most necessary thing that all these various activities within the minister's department be correlated and that


every consideration be given to every aspect of a problem before a final decision is made. I just ask the minister this question. Is it the practice to have the wildlife service represented at conferences making decisions on the development of water resources?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we in the department do not take decisions on the development of water resources in the provinces. I do not agree with the hon. member when he says that the wildlife division in the department is nothing but a backwater in the department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I did not go as far as that, Mr. Chairman; I said that it functions somewhat in the backwaters-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Then let us say "somewhat".

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Oh, in the public mind. I was going to say that in the figures in the estimates that I have in front of me, the total estimates for the wildlife division in 1943-44 were $46,000. This year the total estimates are $472,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am highly pleased to see that, Mr. Chairman. But just to follow the matter up, may I say this. I understand that-in fact I should say that I know it- the minister's department does not make decisions. However, it does discuss possibilities. Obviously the minister's officials came to a definite conclusion as to the propriety of a certain development in British Columbia. But while his department does not make decisions, I think it would be a good idea to have the practice of this department meeting in conference so that all aspects of the problem would be considered when they were even possibly making recommendations or coming to conclusions among themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am not sure that the hon. member realizes that we have no wildlife officers in British Columbia other than those connected with the administration of Migratory Birds Convention Act. In British Columbia wildlife is a provincial responsibility. It is a provincial responsibility, as are waterpower development and forestry. Our wildlife people co-operate with the provinces. They also have to look after the migratory birds convention application in Canada and they have to deal with wildlife in the territories which are ours north of the 60th parallel-that is in the Yukon and Northwest Territories-and also in the national parks.

But the problems of wildlife in the provinces are a provincial responsibility. However, I may say that whenever we have to take a decision which is our decision and which could affect wildlife, of course Mr. Mair, the chief of the wildlife division and his associates are consulted by us, that is by the various branches of the department including the forestry branch, the water resources branch and the deputy minister's office. This applies whenever we have to take a decision on something that could affect wildlife anywhere in Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I just want to follow that up with an illustration where one of the ministers' officials did perform a very useful service two or three years ago. There was an application before the international joint commission to drain what was known as Duck lake for agricultural purposes. It was the evidence, I think, of the department's chief wildlife officer at that time and his obvious mastery of the situation that obviously had some influence on the decision of the international joint commission-that was in British Columbia-in regard to the wildlife and in relation to the interference with a water resource in the province. We appreciated that very much indeed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I was very much interested in hearing the minister say, in connection with the conservation of wildlife, that his department worked in conjunction with the provinces. I think that is quite understandable because wildlife does not recognize provincial boundaries.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Not even international boundaries.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Nor international boundaries. He mentioned the parasite infection of the caribou. In my province we are very much interested, for instance, in the moose herds, and I was wondering what success his department was having in dealing with this parasite infestation of the caribou and whether they found that the moose herds in the northern part of this country were being depleted on account of parasites. I am wondering whether the provinces and his department are working in conjunction in research, for instance, that might deal with this very serious problem, because the moose herds are being wiped out, except in Saskatchewan, where I understand they have opened the season after a good many years of closing. Could the minister give us some idea of what is being done?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I shall be very frank and I shall read the note I have here. I am no expert either on parasites or wildlife, and I
Supply-Northern Affairs do not believe I could be expected to do more than offer the information I have here. Parasites may have an adverse effect on caribou population, but the information available is insufficient to make definite statements.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister what research is being carried out by his department?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources

speechtext: Mr. Mair, who is the chief of the wildlife division, says that it is a continuing research program by the Canadian wildlife service and that some research is also done in various provinces and there is constant exchange of information between the provincial and federal authorities in this matter.
