maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
When this item was discussed last year I had something I wished to say but I happened to be absent from the house and missed the opportunity. However, the member for Kootenay West brought up the subject to which I now wish to refer for a few moments, that is, the question of man's inhumanity to wild life. I refer to the method that we have used for many years to trap our fur-bearing animals.
I do not think that many people other than those who are actually doing the trapping realize the terrible torture that is inflicted

Supply-Northern Affairs on our fur-bearing animals when they are caught in steel traps. As you know, the trapping is all done during the cold winter months, and when an animal is caught it may not die for a matter of days. It will-slowly starve to death, and there is a long story that I cannot go into at this time, telling of this terrible suffering that they put up with. There are millions of these animals killed by the use of traps every year, and, if all their suffering could be added up, people would be so incensed that something would be done to put a stop to it.
One of the big problems has been to find some method of getting these animals and getting their furs in a more humane mariner. After the hon. member for Kootenay West spoke last year, I said that his speech was an effective speech, and it was so much so that he received a very interesting letter from the minister, who showed his interest in this matter. I want to quote from that letter:
From time to time we have received representations against the use of steel traps from humane societies and other organizations. The problem is a difficult one and so far it has not been possible to do away with the use of steel traps, not because of any lack of sympathy with the aim of avoiding unnecessary cruelty, but because no practical solution to the problem has been found. As you pointed out in your remarks, "it is not so easy to find a replacement as one might imagine if one has had no experience in that line."
For many years efforts have been made by a number of societies in Canada and the United States toward more humane practices in trapping and prizes have been offered for the invention of improved traps. There has been little progress in this direction, usually the attempted improvement has been found to be considerably less efficient, difficult to use or much more costly to manufacture. Those interested in the fur trade have also tried to evolve more humane and more efficient equipment. No practical alternative for the steel trap has yet been produced in Canada and its use, therefore, continues to be general throughout the country. I might add that a Mr. Frank Conibear, a former resident and trapper in the Northwest Territories for many years, has been experimenting with an improved type of trap, which he claims would be more humane and more efficient. We have asked the warden service in the Northwest Territories to assist in arranging and assessing field tests of Mr. Conibear's trap . . .
This department is in complete sympathy with the views which you have expressed. I hope that a trap can be found which fulfills, as far as possible, the requirement for humane treatment of animals and which, at the same time, meets the needs of those who must follow the trapline for a living. Difficulties can be expected in getting the trappers, particularly the natives, to adopt any trap which is either inefficient, cumbersome or difficult to use. For that reason, I am glad to know that other types of traps have been found satisfactory in the Scandinavian countries and Germany. We will pursue the matter and I am grateful to Mr. Campbell and yourself for bringing this information to my attention.
The minister speaks there of the efforts that have been made by Mr. Conibear to

develop a more humane trap. I have a news letter which was sent out by the Association for the Protection of Fur-bearing Animals.
This is an organization with headquarters in Vancouver. They talk about this new trap that Mr. Conibear has developed and they say:
There have been setbacks encountered in the past months. First, there was some unavoidable delay in having the traps ready in time, and, on account of the abnormally early winter, this meant that some of the trappers who had promised to try out the traps had to leave for the hills before the traps could reach them, and so they are unable to test them this winter. Mr. Collier, who is president of the B.C. registered trappers association, has now taken all the traps himself, and be and his son are working with them this season. First reports were disappointing on account of some trouble with the trigger, which made the traps hard to set in zero weather. Now, however, adjustments have been made and the last lot of traps have gone out with an improved trigger which has proved entirely satisfactory. The last report we had from Mr. Collier was extremely hopeful.
Then they go and report later that the traps have been proving very successful. I could take a lot of time to give a complete report to the committee on the traps up to date, but I do not want to do that this afternoon. The last thing that is written in this report is that Mr. Collier has been successful in getting mink and many other kinds of animals, but he still has to test for beaver.
I am wondering whether the minister has any knowledge of what has been going on in this sort of experimentation? I would suggest to him that if this new trap proves to be a success he might institute a program somewhat similar to the program that has been used in the province of Quebec in the changing of sap buckets. We all know that the sap producers in the province of Quebec receive some help in exchanging their old sap buckets for a newer kind. I was hoping that if this trap proves to be a success the minister might develop some kind of a scheme whereby the trappers could get some assistance in making the change so that it would not be too hard on them. I would be interested to hear the minister's comment and whether he has any further information regarding this trap or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Here is the up-to-date information I have on this new trap:
Arrangements were made for the warden service in the territories to assist in arranging and assessing field tests of Mr. Conibear's trap. Mr. Conibear had also arranged for field tests to be conducted in British Columbia, Ontario, and some of the states of the United States of America. Reports received from Fort Simpson and Wood Buffalo park were very favourable concerning the use of Mr. Conibear's trap which the trappers agreed killed the animals immediately, but, an adverse report was received from Aklavik. British Columbia also reported quite favourably on the

use of this trap but in all instances it was suggested that further tests be held this coming winter with many more traps of varying sizes. Mr. Conibear has agreed to furnish sufficient traps of different sizes for use next winter on all species of fur-bearing animals and the results of these tests should prove conclusively whether or not Mr. Conibear has succeeded in producing a more humane type of trap which could be adopted generally.

Mr. Chairman, I am going to try an innovation this afternoon and speed up proceedings by making two speeches at once. I am speaking in my own behalf and in behalf of my colleague, the hon. member for Perth, who is in the banking and commerce committee, but we both have the same problem. But I should like to urge upon the minister that he do his very best to persuade his colleagues on the treasury benches to put up the money to complete this project.
As I understand it, the water conservation and flood control-although the water
Supply-Northern Affairs conservation aspect is the aspect that concerns us in this house-works on the Thames river are intended to serve as a sort of prototype for similar works on other rivers. We all know that in this country at the present time, particularly in heavily populated rural and industrial areas such as southern Ontario, the water problem has become a very big thing indeed. Rivers are being drained for irrigation, and during the summer-I grant you, probably not as much this summer as in others as we have had an unusual amount of rainfall this year-water supplies in urban areas which have greatly increased in population have become a very serious problem. I know in southern Ontario it is almost certain that water will have to be piped in from the great lakes to the inland industrial cities such as Kitchener, London, Quelph, and so on.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Not Guelph; we have all kinds of water in Guelph. We do not want any industries that are thinking of coming to Guelph to believe that there is not plenty of water there for them. There is plenty there.

speechtext:
I am glad to hear the hon. member for Wellington South say that he has such an adequate supply of water, and that they will not have the problem that other cities have. I was just using his city an as example. I believe his city must be the only one so situated, with the possible exception of my own.
The water problem is a very large problem in southern Ontario, and the minister and officials of his department are well aware of it. Certain works have, of course, been completed on the Thames valley project, such as the Fanshawe dam near London and the channel improvement scheme near Ingersoll, Ontario. But really, if this very extensive water conservation project is to work, all the dams and other projects must be completed to find out. If it works as well as I believe it is expected it will, then similar projects no doubt will be instituted in other parts of the country that have the same problem. To complete the work on the upper Thames valley authority, the following dams are required to be completed: Glengowan dam and reservoir; Wildwood dam and reservoir; Thamesford dam and reservoir; Woodstock dam and reservoir; Cedar Creek dam and reservoir; St. Marys channel improvement scheme; Mitchell channel improvement scheme. On this item, Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the minister if he would give us some information regarding the proposed inter-governmental meeting between representatives of this government and the government of the United States at which, as the Prime Minister informed us earlier in the session, it is expected that the matter of the Columbia river basin will be discussed.
As I understand it, the reason why this inter-governmental conference will be discussing this matter is because it is considered at the present time that something of an impasse has been reached in the international joint commission. That is to say, the views held by the Canadian section and the United States section do not appear to be capable of reconciliation with reference to the particular subject of the possible diversion of the Columbia river or a substantial part of it through a tunnel below the Mica Creek dam or from a point between the Mica Creek dam and Revelstoke and thus down the Fraser river system.
I should like to know just what importance the government of Canada attaches to that

diversion, not to our right to make it but to the diversion itself, because recently there have been so many conflicting statements as to whether it would ever be possible to construct power dams on the Thompson and Fraser rivers down which those diverted waters would flow without irreparable damage to the fisheries interests. I think we should know now whether the view of the government is that those interests can be reconciled.
The minister was kind enough to give me an interview earlier this session which I would only refer to in general terms. As a result of that interview, however, and as a result of what has already appeared in the press, it is obvious that the fisheries interests up to date, so far as my information goes, are unalterably opposed to the erection of power dams on the Fraser river below Lytton and on the Thompson river between the outlet of Kamloops lake and its junction with the Fraser at Lytton, whereas the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources under the direction of the minister has extended something in the neighbourhood of a quarter of a million dollars to study the power potential of that system in the light of the proposed Columbia diversion.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Not only that; not only the power potential. The contract we have given to B.C. Engineering is to make a complete survey as to the economic feasibility of the diversion, and I have not yet received a report

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No. I have a copy of the contract with the British Columbia Engineering Corporation dated June 14, 1955 and the contract price is shown as $241,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The point I am most concerned with is whether there is any possibility of reconciliation, because up to date the fisheries have been saying, "No dams"; they have been saying they will never agree to the construction of dams on the Columbia and Fraser rivers because they say it cannot be done without irreparable damage to the fisheries interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The matter is presently under scientific study, as the hon. member knows.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I know it is under scientific
study, but statements have been made that those concerned are not now contemplating the erection of power dams on those rivers for that reason. I have seen those statements. The government of the province of British Columbia has taken the position, publicly at any rate, that at the present time it is opposed to the erection of these dams. I should like
Supply-Northern Affairs to know just what is the position so far as the two departments of this government are concerned.
Then I should like to know also the stand this government intends to take at the intergovernmental conference with United States representatives. As the committee knows, the United States has expressed the gravest concern at the possibility of Canada diverting a very substantial portion of the waters of the Columbia down the Thompson and Fraser river systems. General McNaughton has rendered a most outstanding service to this country in the skilful and comprehensive manner in which he has developed Canada's case and placed it before the international joint commission, resting it on the provisions of the international boundary waters treaty and completing it to the point where it is established clearly and absolutely that Canada has the undeniable right to divert these waters within our territory.
That being the position we have taken, then what is the purpose of the inter-governmental discussion? I think the committee is entitled to have from the minister assurance as to the position he intends to take. I hope and I imagine and I expect that it will be that Canada intends to give up nothing, to make no concessions which will in any way jeopardize our right to make this diversion. It has occurred to me that one of the things which should be mentioned in the course of these discussions with the United States-I suppose this must have occurred to those concerned but I have not seen it mentioned very prominently anywhere-is that the United States without any discussion or consent on the part of Canada so obstructed the Columbia river by their dams that they ruined that fishery. We have been most careful to conserve the Fraser system fisheries and to rehabilitate them to the point where they are now most valuable assets, the proceeds of which the United States share to a considerable extent.
I think that that must be borne in mind should any discussion arise as to intransigence or lack of co-operation or unilateral action on the part of the two governments. It is my view that if there has been such intransigence or lack of co-operation it has lain pretty well exclusively in the past on the side of the United States and not on the side of Canada.
I should like to have from the minister the assurance that the studies being carried on by the British Columbia engineering corporation on the Thompson in connection with this diversion and in connection with the power sites on the Thompson and Fraser are being

Supply-Northern Affairs carried on in a realistic manner. I should like to know what additional funds if any are being provided in order to expedite research into the problem of getting spawning fish up and fingerlings down, over or around power dams. In my view there has not been anything like sufficient energy and funds expended on this most important research.
Secondly, I should like to hear when it is expected that the survey with regard to power being carried on by that engineering corporation will be concluded. Thirdly, I should like to hear, and I hope in considerable detail, just what position this government is going to take in the conference with the United States government on this particular subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Kamloops has touched upon one of the most important matters, if not the most important, which I and my associates in the department will have to deal with in the next few months. It is most important, not only for British Columbia but for the whole of Canada because other provinces have rivers which cross the boundary. I agree that the international rivers in British Columbia have the greatest power potential. I can well understand the concern of the hon. member for Kamloops, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, the hon. member for Kootenay West and the hon. member for Kootenay East over the development of the Columbia river, and we should not forget the Yukon river as well.
I understand their concern and I share that concern with them. Dealing with the Columbia, with which the hon. member has dealt, I want to see the optimum economic development of that river in the national interest of Canada and of the province of British Columbia. The hon. member for Kamloops has asked me what importance we attach to the right to divert the waters of the Columbia river to the Fraser river and what importance we attach to the fact of the diversion itself.
As to the right of diversion, we have contended and I contend this afternoon, along with General McNaughton, for whom I think everyone here has such respect, that we have a complete right to divert under article 2 of the treaty of 1909. I believe we have the right to make that diversion if it is economically feasible to do so.
Then the question is asked whether we attach much importance to the diversion itself. We do attach great importance to it if it is in the interest of Canada, if it is economically feasible, and if it is proved that there is no other way of proceeding which would bring better results and greater benefits. I believe that is quite clear.


The hon. member wishes to know whether in the view of the government the fish and power interests can be reconciled. In the over-all study of the possibilities of the diversion the cost of the diversion is a factor, the amount of power which can be developed is a factor, the disruption of certain essential services along the Fraser is a factor, and of course the fisheries are a primary factor. But it is a factor which has to be taken into account in the over-all study of the economic feasibility of the diversion, and that is why this report on fisheries was made, for the benefit of those who make the study on the economic feasibility of a diversion. I do not remember the exact wording in the report that I see the hon. member for Kamloops has in his hands now, but it is said, I believe, that at the present time it would be difficult, if not impossible, to have a series of dams on the Fraser without killing the fisheries. But that is not necessarily the final word, and evidence of that can be found in the fact that some studies are going on at the University of British Columbia and that studies are being made constantly and continually in the Department of Fisheries on the possibility of having the fingerlings and other fish go over the dams.
As we say in French it is a verite de La Palice, that science is improving all the time, and it may very well be that in the very near future some ways and means will be found of overcoming these difficulties. Why should we discard these possibilities? I believe that no possibility should be discarded. We talk about the differences in views and the differences between the fisheries and the power interests. Of course there are differences between the fish and the power interests, and of course we hope it may be possible to reconcile them if we study more deeply the problem that is presented. But to say immediately that we should stop any economic study of the diversion because at the present time we do not have sufficient scientific knowledge of how to cope with the fisheries problem is, I believe, not reasonable.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I believe so too, and I hope the minister is not suggesting that we are saying anything different. It is his colleague, the Minister of Fisheries, who has been saying it.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I do not agree with the hon. member that the Minister of Fisheries has said that at no time could there be any reconciliation. I do not agree with the hon. member. The Minister of Fisheries has not said that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
May I refer to page 43 of the report where I find the following:
Since one ot the alternate routes for diverting Columbia river water into Shuswap lake is by way of the Seymour river it can be stated that the environmental change in the spawning and incubation area will be so severe that the existing run of sockeye will be exterminated.
That deals only with one particular part of-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
That only deals with one way of developing the Fraser, by ten dams. There may be all kinds of other ways which no doubt will be visualized in the report we expect from the B. C. Engineering Corporation. No, there is no final impossibility of reconciliation, and I am sure that the Minister of Fisheries would agree with what I say now. There is no insurmountable difficulty that I can foresee.
Finally, the hon. member for Kamloops asked me what stand we intend to take in our negotiations with the United States in the matter of rivers crossing the international boundary. In answer I have to put a question to the hon. member. I do not know if he is a poker player. I have played quite a bit in my life but never with my hand face up on the table.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I think the minister has already answered the question in part and to that extent has put his hand face up on the table. I do not think it will weaken his bargaining position because he has told us that we take the stand most definitely that we have the right to make this diversion. He has indicated that we are not going to depart from that position. I suppose if it comes to the point where the United States is going to make us some offer in terms of return of power if we will abandon not the right to do it but indicate that we do not intend to exercise that right, it then becomes a question of negotiation. But I cannot at the moment foresee any return or promise they could make to us, in the light of our present limited knowledge of the potentialities of that diversion, which we would be justified in accepting as full compensation not only for now but for the future for what might be the potentialities to us of our development of the Columbia river. Therefore my view at present would be, and I urge this upon the minister-perhaps it will strengthen his hand when it is dealt-that because of the lack of definite knowledge of what this might mean to Canada when this potential is developed there should be no concession made to the United States. I do not think we are in a position to know what we would be giving up if we agreed now to give up anything in terms of potential development.
Supply-Northern Affairs
I do not see how the minister can take any other position and in fact protect Canada's rights, as he has said he is concerned to do, and as I know he is concerned to do. Therefore I do not see that there is much bargaining that can actually be done. I think we have to say something to them to this effect: You can rely on us, whenever and however we exercise our rights, to exercise them first from the point of view of Canada's interests as the paramount consideration but then to exercise them, of course, in such a manner that they will inflict the least possible damage or disadvantage upon you, and that we will at all times be ready to discuss modifications of our plans whenever the time comes to implement them.
I do not think we can go any farther than that at the present time because I believe we might be placing ourselves in the position where we did not think we would be giving up anything of real value but might find in 10 or 15 years that we had parted with an interest or a right or an opportunity which in the intervening years had become most valuable, valuable beyond anything that we think at present it would represent.
As to the fisheries, Mr. Chairman, I am glad to hear what the minister said with regard to his colleague and the Department of Fisheries because it certainly has seemed to me in the past, and I have come to this conclusion in part on the basis of the report which I hold in my hand entitled A Report on the Fish Facilities and Fisheries Problems Related to the Fraser and Thompson River Dam Site Investigations, that the official attitude of the Department of Fisheries was that they were opposed now and for all time not only to discussion of the idea of a diversion but to any further studies and investigations of it. I think the minister would agree with me on reflection that the conclusion to be drawn from a reading of this report in its literal sense is that it is the official view of the Department of Fisheries-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: -that there can be no reconciliation.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is the conclusion that you are drawing.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I say based on the reading of this report and the various sentences, paragraphs and summaries that are contained in it. If the minister tells me that in fact this report is merely a cautionary statement, all right, I hope he is right. I assume if he says so that he bases it on discussions with his colleague and discussions among the departmental officials. I hope he will insist that that is the proper course to follow. To

Supply-Northern Affairs talk in terms of the impossibility of the reconciliation of the interests of fisheries and power would to my mind result in an inevitable and sharp conflict with, I think, only one conclusion, however regrettable that would be, namely that power would win. If there were the creation of a spirit of conflict, I believe the result would be that fisheries would be swept aside and really damaged, and perhaps eliminated.
It is therefore essential that there be cooperation. With the minister I believe that if there is co-operation and effort, and above all effort and work, some way can be devised of having both power and fisheries, and in that way the interests of the two can be reconciled. But without such co-operation, and if any more statements like these are made and public opinion is aroused on one side or the other, it may become impossible to reconcile the two. The public demand for an immediate start on projects for power may be such that, as I say, fisheries will be brushed aside, and that would be a very disastrous development.
The minister mentioned the question of research. Research is being carried on at the University of British Columbia, but the bulk of the contribution is made by private industry. Research is being carried on in the fisheries department.

While I think the British Columbia Power Corporation, which has a very direct interest in this whole development, is to be commended for the money it has made available to the University of British Columbia for the study, I do not think the industry which has such a great stake in the matter has gone any too far. I believe the sum was $50,000. I do not think that is in any way out of proportion on the plus side having regard to the interest which the company has in the problem. I think the fishing industry as well as the department, those interested in power development and government have an obligation to get on with this job of research into the reconciliation of these otherwise conflicting interests.
I should like to hear from the minister also whether, in his discussions with the premier of British Columbia which took place recently, any consideration was given to the setting up of a joint development authority for the Columbia river basin; whether the problem of who is to build the dam at Mica creek was discussed; and whether any mutually acceptable approach was worked out to the question of who will generate the power and where the power will be made available.
There is danger of another conflict of interests. Already the minister's colleague, namely the Minister of Fisheries, has said that he hopes all the power to be developed at Mica creek will be reserved for Vancouver and the lower mainland area. I do not know that it is altogether a proper thing for a federal minister to be saying to which part of a province power will be allocated. The interior of our province, which is rapidly developing-in the Kootenay area where the dam is to be situated and in my own part of the interior-has an industrial potential which most definitely will be in need of power.

I hope we are not going to have a situation where a federal minister is taking the position that only one area of British Columbia should be served by this tremendous project which is actually situated in the other area. It is another case where I think there should be consultation and co-operation, rather than that ministers should be rushing out and taking sides in a conflict over a development that has not even taken place. But since those statements have been made by the Minister of Fisheries I should like the minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources to tell us whether there were discussions with Mr. Bennett on the mutual development of this project, and as to whether there will be any mutual sharing of responsibility in the allocation of the results.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Oxford completed my case for me in a very able manner, but he misdirected his request. I live on the great watershed of the Grand river, on which this government has done a great deal of work. I think I should speak for a minute or two on this item.
It was almost 20 years ago that Dr. Hugh Templin, the editor of the Fergus News Record, started the campaign for control of flooding on the Grand river. As a result he persuaded the minister of works of the provincial government, Brigadier Colin Campbell, who was then a very prominent cabinet minister in Mitchell F. Hepburn's cabinet, to build the first of those control dams, and that was built in my riding just above Fergus. This worked out very successfully and prevented a great deal of the damage which was done annually in the towns of Fergus, Elora, the cities of Galt and Brantford, and on the outskirts of Waterloo and Kitchener.
It was an experiment. Because of that experiment there have been several others built since. The second one was built on the Grand river, in the marshes in Luther. The Luther marshes have been famous in our section of Ontario for a number of years. When I first heard of them the idea was to drain them so we would have more farm

Supply-Northern Affairs land. Now all those drains have been flooded by the second dam built at Luther, and it has created possibly the greatest natural wildlife source in the province. I suppose there is more and better duck hunting in the Luther marshes, because of the work done there jointly by the provincial and federal governments, than anywhere else in Ontario. It is excellent hunting, and we are not depleting the wildlife of the country by shooting the wild fowl that come to the Luther marshes. It is an ideal nesting place, and more ducks are raised in the Luther marshes than are shot. It is not just a case of shooting off the ducks that fly in from the north to rest there on their way south.
The third project on the Grand river watershed has been started at Conestogo, so we have a very complete large dam project on the watershed of the Grand river. I would recommend to the minister that he now do exactly what the hon. member for Oxford suggested should be done, namely complete the control of this watershed.
There is a very good reason why this control should be completed. It is closer to completion than any other watershed control system that is being undertaken anywhere. We should complete the small dams that are waiting to be built on all the small tributaries leading into this watershed. There are two dams which should be built in Eramosa township, near Rochwood to protect Guelph, Hespeler and Preston. When these and some others are built, then we will have a good idea of the type of plan that should be arranged for the other various watersheds in the highly industrialized areas of Ontario.
This brings me to another point mentioned by the hon. member for Oxford, when he said the city of Guelph is short of water. Every city has a problem in finding water for drinking purposes. Guelph happens to be most fortunate in having good springs, and no doubt the flow of water in those springs is added to greatly by those control dams in the watershed close to them. The water table must obviously be raised because of those control dams, and that gives Guelph an excellent supply of spring water. Then they also have deep wells in Guelph to augment the supply of spring water. It is quite logical to say that those deep wells are supplied with water that is held in the ground by those control dams.
I say to the minister that if he is going to complete any watershed with control dams, the logical one is the Grand river watershed. This was promoted extensively by Dr. Hugh Templeton; and the present editor

of the Elora Express, Mrs. Marsden, is now a member of the Grand river authority, and so is the former warden of the county of Wellington, Mr. Norman Williams. They are almost anxious that the project that has pioneered in these control dams be completed first. I could not agree more completely with the hon. member for Oxford in his request that you go ahead and finish this. Certainly the Grand river watershed is the one that has given leadership, and these people should be looked after who have done the spade work in this valuable field of flood control.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps I might be allowed to take one or two minutes in connection with this item. I think my remarks will relate to it.
Last evening I read a very interesting article which appeared in the Toronto Evening Telegram of that date, written by Mr. James M. Minifie. The title of the article is "And Now: The Ultimate Missile". Mr. Minifie was referring to material which apparently he had at his disposal in Washington in connection with the ICBM, the intercontinental ballistic missile, and he referred to the fact that giant strides were being made in connection with a counter missile that would require the very best and latest type of radar detection in order to be put to work.
In his article Mr. Minifie mentioned that minutes would be very vital in connection with the detection of the ICBM by the counter missile, and apparently the indications are that a new D.E.W. line will be required located 500 or 600 miles farther north than the one which is being constructed at the present time. I might read from this article

his reference to the fact that a new D.E.W. line would be required. Mr. Minifie says:
Success in this fantastic project-
That is the development of a counter missile; those are my words, Mr. Chairman. -would have important repercussions in Canada. For one of the essentials would be another D.E.W. line, 500 or 600 miles farther north, running from Ellesmere island westward out over the Arctic ice. This sea area is regarded by Canada as Canadian territory on the sector principle by which eastern and western boundaries are carried northwards to the pole.
The United States however does not recognize this principle, and might not concede Canada's claim if it were formally presented which has not yet been done.
The indication further on in the article is that the chief of research and development of the United States army, Lieutenant General James M. Gavin, is thinking of the same thing because he is quoted as saying:
As we look ahead we see considerable pay-oft in being able to put stations out on the polar ice cap to detect missiles early in their flight, perhaps detect them at the instant of take-off.
The ability to live out there, to reinforce out there, to explore and patrol out there may be of great importance to us in the immediate future in fact.
Mr. Minifie goes on to say:
Thus consideration is being given by the United States armed services to American military occupation of an area which Canada considers its own.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Calgary North dealt with the over-all picture in the northern area, and the fact that there is considerable concern as to the continuation of at least the show of Canadian sovereignty in that area.
We now have an indication that a further step is being planned, and I do not think the hon. member for Calgary North referred to this. Here is a situation in which we are now informed that steps may be required to be taken in the foreseeable future by the country to the south of us in order to provide a form of continental defence for all of us which may bring into dispute two theories concerning the ownership of the polar ice cap north of the Canadian land mass. Mr. Minifie's article indicates that it might be wise to make plans here to ensure that when the time comes there will be no dispute concerning our claims to sovereignty in this area, and to establish it beyond any question of doubt.
I would ask the minister if any steps have been taken to consider this problem, if there have been any discussions between his department and any department in Washington or among his department and any other department of this government and Washington to deal with this particular problem? It seems to me there is no point in waiting until the
Supply-Northern Affairs horse is out of the barn before closing the door. If we are going to be faced with a new D.E.W. line situation our government should now be taking steps to ensure that there is no question about our sovereignty in this particular area. I think we all welcome assistance from the United States in terms of continental defence and it is absolutely essential that we receive it, but I do believe it should be under conditions which are acceptable to the mass of the Canadian people.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: To my knowledge, Mr. Chairman, no approach has been made by the United States government to the Canadian government for another defence line to the north of the D.E.W. line.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Has there been any discussion of the principle of ownership of the ice cap north of the land area where, according to the indication in this article, we assert one principle and the United States asserts another?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: We have never subscribed to the sector theory in application to the ice. We are content that our sovereignty exists over all the Arctic islands. There is no doubt about it and there are no difficulties concerning it. Our sovereignty has never been endangered by the existence of the D.E.W. line. We have agreements with the United States and the facts are there to prove we have sovereignty over our northern territory. We have never upheld a general sector theory. To our mind the sea, be it frozen or in its natural liquid state, is the sea; and our sovereignty exists over the lands and over our territorial waters.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Do I gather from the minister's answer that if the situation were reversed and it was Russia which intended to make use of this area for a warning line of some kind, we would not be concerned because that does not affect our principle of ownership?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: As far as we are aware, Russia has never claimed water or ice as being in the territory over which it has sovereignty. I have not heard that the United States wants to establish a line on the ice cap north of the islands of Canada because this area is the high sea, be it frozen or in liquid form. I suppose and I certainly hope that my hon. friend believes in the freedom of the high seas.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I do not think there is any question about the freedom of the high seas. What I am requesting from the minister is an answer to a simple question. If we do not assert the sector principle which has been referred to in this article,

Supply-Northern Affairs does that mean that we are quite satisfied to have any power occupy the polar ice cap north of our territory?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The ice cap is in exactly the same situation as the Atlantic ocean; it is the high sea.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The minister has not answered the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The hon. member can answer it himself. I have indicated the principles. I do not have to apply them for you.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I think the minister is evading the question. There is no use saying that the polar ice cap is the high seas because it is not. You cannot sail a ship over it or anything else. As he probably knows, permanent establishments have been erected on the ice cap in the way of landing fields, radar stations and so on. As the minister also probably knows, at the present time a big scramble is going on among half a dozen countries to establish sovereignty over various parts of the Antarctic ice cap.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: There is land there.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Some of it is land.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It is a continent.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Nobody knows.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is the difference.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Nobody knows. The minister says there is land, but nobody knows just how much is land. It is an ice cap; nevertheless nations are attempting to establish sovereignty over parts of that ice cap. As far as this Arctic ice cap is concerned, nobody knows how much of it is water and how much of it is land. I do not think it is good enough for the minister to evade this question by saying that these are the high seas. They are not. This is an ice cap upon which permanent installations have been established and supplied by air transport.

Mr. Chairman, I was just pointing out that at page 42 there is another more detailed map, and it shows the same thing. It shows the boundary running right up to the north pole along the longitude separating Alaska and the Yukon, and then coming back down again between our northern islands and Greenland and then down to the tip of Labrador. I do not think there is any question that the Canadian government, in the making of its maps and so forth, has tacitly at least given adherence to the sector theory of the possession of this northern area. I think the minister is in error when he says the Canadian government has not adopted that theory and that it has been more or less taken for granted.
Some two years ago I raised this matter in connection with an ice island, I think it was, which some Soviet scientists were occupying and which was floating around up in this northern area. I wanted to know at that time what the situation was, whether Canada exercised any sovereignty over it and so on, and at that time no question was raised as to Canada's sovereignty over this sector extending right up to the north pole. From what the minister has said today, apparently without saying anything to anybody the government is going to abandon that theory altogether and thus perhaps put us in a very awkward position as far as bargaining with any foreign power is concerned.
As the hon. member for York West has pointed out, if the Americans want to put radar stations there we will be delighted and have no objection to it, but if the Russians or somebody else wanted to do the same

Supply-Northern Affairs thing it would be a totally different matter. In order to protect ourselves I think we should certainly return to what I have always understood was our theory of sovereignty there, the sector theory, and assert our sovereignty over that sector extending up to the north pole as, indeed, it is shown on both maps in this publication on the boundaries of Canada by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.
Furthermore, before the minister makes the statement that we do not claim any sovereignty over that area, I think he should consult the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys under whose authority these maps are issued and also the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the other members of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I do not need to consult with my colleagues, because the government of Canada has never adhered to the general sector theory.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: May I ask the minister, then, why maps are put out showing this as Canadian territory?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
If I am given time I will tell you. In 1903 these lines were put on the maps of Canada for the first time. It was not to show the boundaries of Canada. It was to show the lines within which the lands and the territorial waters around those lands were claimed by Canada, because at that time and for a number of years afterwards many of the islands of the Arctic had not been discovered and it was not known what islands might exist in the interior of that sector.
Our claim since 1903 has been to all the land within these lines, but we have never adhered to a broader sector theory. If you adhere to the general sector theory you claim that you have sovereignty over waters beyond your territorial waters. We have never done that. It is said that because it is ice we might claim sovereignty over it, but the ice is moving all the time. It is never the same ice. Do you believe that any country in the world would recognize our sovereignty over the air space above this water in its liquid or frozen form? If you claim sovereignty over a piece of land or your territorial waters, you also have sovereignty over the air space above that land and territorial waters. Other countries would never recognize our sovereignty over these high seas, be they in liquid or frozen form, and which in the frozen form are moving all the time.
That is the law. That is what the position of the Canadian government has been all

the time. I do not need to consult my colleagues, but I believe the member for Calgary North would have done well if he had consulted someone before asserting the things he has asserted without knowing what he was talking about.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The minister has not explained why all the maps show it in that way. I only mentioned two of them but there are a dozen more.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I just said that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You did not explain why all these maps show that area as part of Canada. Here is one found on page 112 of Geographical Regions of Canada. The whole area from the north pole down to the Mackenzie area and from there over to Labrador is shown as the Arctic area, and it goes right up to the north pole. Every other map in the book shows the same thing.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I think what we have seen here is an example of an assertion of a principle established over a period of years which, if allowed to continue in a laissez-faire manner, will result in our being confronted with a very serious situation. The minister has said that no country would recognize the assertion of our sovereignty in this particular instance. I say to the minister that with conditions changing, with the present use of air transport in the northern areas, and the fact that an ice cap of this kind may be very useful for detection purposes in warfare and even useful for emergency landings of civil air transports, it is time we as one of the major northern powers took steps to ensure that this type of sovereignty is recognized. If we do not, we will be left with no alternative if an unfriendly power steps in and says it is going to make use of the ice cap for offensive purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It is not an ice cap. This is floating ice which is moving all the time. Any establishment that you might put on that ice could not last for very long. It could not be permanent because the ice is melting, floating and breaking all the time. This is not an ice cap like the ice cap of Greenland. This is ice floating on water.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
On the 22nd of June last the hon. member for Brandon-Souris and myself raised a question with regard to Mr. Fontana of Virden, Manitoba, and his claim for redress for certain mineral rights which were taken into the ownership of the crown. At

that tune the Minister of Finance, who was leading the house said, as found at page 5314 of Hansard:
I can assure hon. members, in particular the hon. member for Brandon-Souris and the hon. member for Dauphin, who have spoken on one particular matter, that it will receive serious consideration and an answer will be given at the appropriate time.
I understand this is the appropriate time. I know that very serious consideration has been given, and we are anxiously waiting for the minister to inform the committee that the government, in its wisdom and generosity, has decided to accede to the request of Mr. Fontana.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I believe I am ready to reply to the pleas made by the member for Brandon-Souris and the member for Dauphin when they spoke in the house some weeks ago. The land, 320 acres, owned by Mr. Fontana was required for an airport near the town of Virden in Manitoba for the purposes of the commonwealth air training scheme. The land department of the Canadian National Railways acted as agents for the government in acquiring the land.
In August, 1940, an agent of the company interviewed Mr. Fontana and obtained an option dated August 7, 1940, signed by him and his wife, agreeing to sell the land for $9,000. There were no exceptions mentioned in the written documents. In recommending the acceptance of the offer to his superiors at Winnipeg, the agent expressed the view that while the assessed value of the land was only $5,900-that was $5,200 for the land and $700 for the building-the price asked by Mr. Fontana was not unreasonable.
Although the Department of Transport filed a plan of expropriation on November 2, 1940, there is nothing on the files of the railway company to indicate that when Fontana agreed to the price three months before, there had been any threat of compulsory taking or that he was influenced by it.
Following the signing of the option, the completion of the transaction was handled by the company's lawyers at Winnipeg, who dealt with Mr. J. Pritchard, a lawyer at Virden who acted for Mr. Fontana. Some delay occurred because part of the land was registered in the name of a third party from whom he had purchased, and with the consent of Fontana some of the purchase moneys had to be paid to him. When these difficulties had been arranged, Fontana executed a transfer under the real property act in favour of His Majesty. This transfer was prepared in the office of Mr. Pritchard and signed by Mr. Fontana in his presence on November 6, 1940. The transfer covered the complete interest of Mr. Fontana and contained no reservations. 67509-442
Supply-Northern Affairs
I have inquired about the matter. I know that in the province of Quebec, according to our civil law-and I am told by the lawyers I have consulted that the situation is the same under the common law-whenever you purchase land, you purchase the land-and I am translating word for word the expression in the civil code-with what is under and what is above unless something either under or above is excepted. When you purchase land and there is no reservation you purchase the land with everything which is under and everything which is above.
The transfer was registered and the certificate or title was issued in favour of His Majesty for the land, including the mineral rights. Of course it included the mineral rights because they were not excepted. The balance of the purchase moneys to which Fontana was entitled was then sent to his solicitor, who acknowledged them on December 14, 1940. I believe it is worth quoting the receipt. It reads as follows:
Re Virden Airport-August Fontana Your reference 22-302-34-B
This will acknowledge receipt of your letter herein of the 13th instant, inclosing cheque in favour of August Fontana for the sum of $3 694 m full settlement of all his claims in the above connection, and for which kindly accept my thanks.
J. Pritchard.
It was not until March, 1954-that is to say nearly 15 years later-that Mr. Fontana, through his solicitor, made a claim* for the mineral rights. This was some time after oil had been discovered in the Virden district. In view of the claim made by Mr. Fontana^ the question of the title to the mines and minerals was referred to the justice department which expressed the opinion that Fontana had no claim in law for their return.
Mr. Fontana and the person from whom the adjoining section, which was needed to make up the airport, had been acquired, each filed a petition in the exchequer court claiming that they had not been compensated for the minerals, that it was not the intention of the crown to acquire them, and that they should be held in trust for the petitioners. Motions were made by the crown to strike out both petitions on the ground that they were frivolous and vexatious. The court granted the orders. Fontana appealed to the supreme court but his appeal was dismissed.
The applications to the exchequer court and the supreme court were both made on the ground that, assuming the allegations in the petition were correct, there was no arguable cause of action. The courts agreed with that view. The legal ownership of the mineral rights has therefore been finally determined. It should also be mentioned that nearly all

Supply-Northern Affairs the grounds upon which the present petition is based were contained in the material before the two courts.
Notwithstanding the decision of the courts Mr. Fontana, through his solicitor, filed another petition addressed to His Excellency the Governor General and to me, claiming practically the same relief. The cabinet has studied the petition very carefully and has rejected it because there were no grounds at all for it.
The only thing I want to add is this, and I shall be very brief. Some reference has been made to the Crichel Down case by one or even two hon. members. They have mentioned Crichel Down as being the name of a man. May I say it is not the name of a man; it is the name of a place in the United Kingdom or a locality in the United Kingdom. The case that was dealt with in the British House of Commons was as follows. The land was owned or leased by several persons all of whom died before the matter was discussed in the British house. Some of the executors laid claim to the property but it was never given back to them, because it had already been leased to an outsider and what had been done could not be undone.
The facts of the Crichel Down case are not similar. In that case the land was no longer required for government purposes. In our case it is still required for government purposes because the Department of Transport still owns and operates the Virden airport. Instead of accepting offers from the previous owners to buy the land back, it was rented to an outsider as a single unit. The previous owners in the British case were not even given a chance to tender. In this case this department publicly advertised the mineral rights for sale. Mr. Fontana had a right to tender and could do so. That was not the case in the British case. It is completely different.
In the Fontana case it is asked that the mineral rights revert to the owner. This was never done in the English case. It was never suggested by anyone in the English case that they would not have to pay the going price when it was resold to them. The view was expressed in the English case that the normal practice would have been to have the tenancy offered for public tender, just as the oil rights in our case have been offered. As a matter of fact, what was contended by the majority of the critics in the Crichel Down case is exactly what we have done here in putting up for public tender the oil rights under the Virden airport.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am glad to have the reply of the minister with regard to this important matter. I anticipated that the reply would
[Mr. Lesage.l
be couched in legal terms, and that has fairly well been the case in the argument of the minister here this afternoon. Harking back to my first presentation of this case on June 22 last, may I say that at that time I stressed the factor of moral obligation with regard to this particular matter of public business. At that time I outlined the three grounds upon which Mr. Fontana had a reasonable claim against the crown.
First of all, he lost his mineral rights by a mere accident of conveyancing. I understand that is a term that has some legal significance. He was asked to surrender his land for wartime purposes and this he did; and by the legal process of conveyancing, unbeknown to Mr. Fontana, he also lost the underground rights. I think that is the first point that is significant in this case.
In the second place, it is quite obvious that when the crown-through Mr. Johnston, working in the C.N.R. lands branch-approached Mr. Fontana, the mineral rights were not required. The surface rights only were required for the purpose of establishing an air training field under the commonwealth airtraining scheme.
Third, Mr. Fontana was never compensated in any shape or form for other than the surface rights. He received the sum of $9,000 for the land, and that was merely for surface rights. The minerals, according to the statement of Mr. Johnston, who carried out the transaction on behalf of the government, were not in question. We have a letter from Mr. Johnston, dated December 6, 1955, in which he says:
At that time mineral rights were not considered of any particular value and were not a factor in arriving at a valuation for the acreage. Some mention was made of sand and gravel and, to the best of my recollection, Mr. Fontana had promised delivery of some sand or gravel and it was suggested he had better remove same before acceptance of his offer to sell by the crown.
In other words Mr. Johnston, who carried out the negotiations with Mr. Fontana, acknowledges that the evaluation of minerals was not a consideration at the time. So on the basis of these three factors I submit that there is strong moral obligation involved in the case.
There are some legal rights as well, the minister in his reply has suggested that the matter was considered by the courts, both the exchequer court and the Supreme Court of Canada. However, from the evidence in the return tabled on June 25, return No. 243, it is quite clear that at no time were the merits of the case reviewed by either of those courts; rather it was the petition of the crown to have the appeal to the courts struck out that was considered. The motion by the crown

was to the effect that this appeal was vexatious and frivolous, and it was on those grounds that the courts turned down the appeal.
I think there is an important principle at stake in this regard. It is obvious that even in democratic countries power is passing from the courts to the departments of government at an alarming rate, and I feel that this is a principle that arises in this instance. If this had been a private transaction between two private citizens there would have been no way of keeping Mr. Fontana from having the merits of his case considered in the courts, but because the crown was involved this was not possible.
There is also the opinion of legal counsel in this instance. There have been three reputable lawyers involved, as 1 read through the return, in this case.

Three outstanding lawyers were involved in the case; Mr. Harold Riley, Q.C., of Calgary; Mr. E. W. Gerrand, Q.C., of Regina; and Mr. William R. Appleby, of Winnipeg. I understand that all these men are devoted to the cause of pure Liberalism, and I think that it is from that standpoint that they have reviewed the merits of this case. I believe the men in question will be well known to the minister. In the various presentations they have made to the cabinet they have stressed the legal aspects of the Fontana appeal, particularly the justice of the case. I think I shall just quote one paragraph from a communication that was directed to the Minister of Justice in this regard on May 11, 1955, over the signature of Mr. William R. Appleby. The final paragraph says;
I am writing this letter to you in order that I may request your earnest and serious consideration to a very important problem, one which in my opinion, concerns itself with the very basic principles of government. This certainly is exemplified through the Crichel Down debate in the English House of Commons. May I respectfully suggest that the proper answer to this question is to re-vest the mineral rights in Fontana, pursuant to section 24 of the Expropriation Act. If this were done, I believe that the basic principles of equity and justice according to our law, would be served.
Yours very truly,
(sgd) W. R. Appleby.
The other legal advisers have written in similar vein to Mr. Appleby's letter. I shall not take the time of the house to quote further from their letters, but I must refer briefly to

I am not going to deal further with the Crichel Down case. I thought I would make passing reference to it in view of the minister's observations. There is also this further fact. Most provincial governments have recognized the rights of private citizens in these matters. The minister referred to the situation in the province of Quebec. In the province of Manitoba, on the other hand, the provincial government has now taken the stand, after severe public criticism, that in cases of land expropriation for crown purposes the expropriation would not include the mineral rights. The Manitoba government has gone even farther in this matter and has returned the mineral rights on several parcels of land that were expropriated for rights of way for highways, and so forth. They did so because they could see there was a moral as well as a legal obligation involved in transactions between private citizens and governments in cases of this kind.
Then we have the petition of over 200 citizens of this area intimately in touch with the situation, who had a meeting to consider all the facts. They submitted a petition to the government, which has been placed in the hands of all members of this house. They recognize as private citizens that there is a violation of the rights of the individual citizen, and there is a violation of the elementary justice that we should expect from a democratic government.
Consider the position of Mr. Fontana himself. He is a man well advanced in years. He is an immigrant from Italy who came to Canada in pursuit of the wider opportunities of the new world. He worked hard in railway construction gangs, and in very heavy labour of that kind, to accumulate enough money to buy this parcel of land. He passed through the period of the dirty thirties, and by 1940 he was slowly getting back on his feet again. The government came along and asked that he transfer the land to the crown for defence purposes.
The minister raised the point this afternoon that expropriation action as such was never completely carried out. That was only because of Mr. Fontana's patriotism. He was only too willing to allow this land to be used for defence purposes. Unfortunately Mr. Fontana, a typical representative of that generation of immigrants, was not literate. He came to Canada and was one of the pioneers of the Virden district. He worked
[Mr. Dinsdale.l
long and hard to establish himself in our Canadian economy; and it is largely on the basis of the blood, sweat and tears of this generation that we today enjoy the privileges and the prosperity that are ours.
He was not aware of the legal niceties of this expropriation procedure. All he could see was the opportunity of expressing his gratitude for the privileges Canada had granted to him and his family as a naturalized citizen here. Both he and his wife had to sign the documents with an X; but we have the confirmation of Mr. Johnston, who carried out the negotiations, that while Mr. Fontana did not inquire about minerals Mr. Johnston himself, because of the inquiry concerning the gravel, assured him that minerals were not involved.
I pursue this subject this afternoon, Mr. Chairman, because I feel it is a case of a further invasion of the rights of private citizens by big government. We cannot compare this with a transaction that would take place between private citizen and private citizen. This is a transaction that took place during the exigencies of war between the government and a private citizen.
