speechtext: -merely the motion that it be stricken out as frivolous and vexatious.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is what it was. That is the decision.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: But let me carry on, notwithstanding the noise from the ministers and the backbenchers opposite. Let me conclude the point I started to make.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
On a point of order, I dissociate myself from the reference to the backbenchers, but I now seriously question

the chairman as to whether the hon. member who spoke last evening on one vote, namely, 294, is really in order now in speaking for such a long time on this matter on the present vote under consideration?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I spoke on the first item last evening, sir.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Are you repeating your speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You are repeating your speech.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The first item allows an hon. member the opportunity to discuss policy. In view of the fact that the minister has spoken on this item I think I should have the opportunity to reply.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It is the third time you have made the same speech.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
There are one or two
interesting additional items that I should like to bring to the attention of the senior member for Halifax.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
It
takes a long time to get the point across.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Obviously it takes hon. members opposite a long 'time to get the point. I am surprised that hon. members opposite, who are nominally Liberals, are not willing to listen to the presentation of a case which has been supported by three Liberal lawyers in this country as having a bearing on the fundamental rights of an individual citizen. If the rights of a private member in this house are to be denied by the government backbenchers, I think parliamentary democracy has descended to a very low level. I am trying to present the reason-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Just Conservative backbenchers, that is all.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I would suggest there is no noise at all coming from the backbenchers of the opposition. All the noise is coming from the back benches on the government side of the house. I am speaking on behalf of over 200 citizens who have presented a petition to every hon. member of this house.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No, you are not; you are just speaking for one of your constituents.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: They have presented a petition to this house.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The hon. member has tried my patience too far.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is too bad.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I would suggest that the hon. member-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
-pick up his marbles and go home.
Supply-Northern Affairs

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: He has no marbles.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: -read the Crichel Down debate which took place in the British House of Commons. It occupied almost a day and it was on a point as simple as the one we have before this house, as is suggested by some hon. members; the point of the fundamental rights of a private citizen. I think that is deserving of even greater consideration than the rights of an overwhelmingly powerful government. However, let us carry on with the discussion.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes, let us get On with it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Under the Expropriation Act, in cases of expropriation the person affected, as I read the act and have had it interpreted to me, should be left as nearly as possible in the same position as his neighbours. This being so, Mr. Fontana should be restored to a position of equality with his neighbours who are enjoying their rights because their lands were never required for war purposes. It might be argued that this establishes an unfortunate precedent, but if that is the case I would say it is a good precedent, because justice, freedom and liberty have already been damaged to a considerable extent in this country.
We have moved far along the road of arbitrary government action. Perhaps in view of the comments we have heard during this discussion this afternoon I might urge the supporters of the government and the people of Canada to appeal to the Prime Minister that justice in this instance might prevail.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I would like to ask the minister one question. In his remarks a few moments ago he mentioned that the mineral rights have been offered for public tender in this case.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I wonder if the minister could state just when this was done?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Sometime in 1955; I do not recall the exact date.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: May I ask what were the results of that offer?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The highest tenderer tendered for $200,000, but it was not only for the minerals on the property about which the hon. members have been talking. There was also an adjoining property of the same size.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The reason I ask that question is because I think the very reply the minister has just given pretty well takes the rug out from under his feet so far as the argument he has been using in reply to the representations we are making is concerned.

Supply-Northern Affairs
The minister rested his case largely on the fact that the government is justified in the attitude it is talcing because of the fact that after the minerals contained in that property were found to be valuable they were offered for public auction, and that Mr. Fontana had the same opportunity to bid-I think I am using the words of the minister-as had anyone else for these mineral rights.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Sure.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: We have to be practical, of course, as well as technical. The minister knows as well as I and as well as the hon. member for Brandon-Souris that Mr. Fontana would stand no chance whatever in attempting to bid for mineral rights in competition with Imperial Oil, British American Oil, Gulf Oil and all the other friends of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What if you had purchased the land?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Would you have given Fontana $200,000 15 years later?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if we could break that duet down to a solo I would be able to answer the questions. There are two hon. gentlemen speaking and I cannot hear either one.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What if you had purchased the land; what would you do?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: If I had sold the land to whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: If you had purchased the land from Mr. Fontana 15 years ago would you feel obligated to give him $200,000 or to give him his mineral rights? I am sure you would not. You would keep them as any man in Canada who has purchased property when there was no reservation of the mineral rights has done in the past.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is not a forced deal. It is the same thing; sure it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: There was no forced sale. You are proving to me this afternoon that you are a very poor lawyer, Hamilton.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Don't be personal, now. This is supposed to be a House of Commons; don't bring personalities into it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am very glad that the minister-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
If the legal talent will hire themselves a hall they can argue this out, and I shall continue to speak in the meantime.
What the minister has just said throws much light on the question. He asked me if I or any private individual for that matter were to purchase that land and a grievance

was raised 15 years later, I would be inclined to take the mineral rights into consideration. What the minister seems to forget is that this is not the case of one private individual purchasing from another. This is a case where the government approached a private individual and at first threatened expropriation. The government found later that it was not necessary to go through with the expropriation, and it purchased the property for an airport which was used for war purposes. When the war was over the property was no longer required for that purpose.
I think the minister was not quite accurate when he said the government still operates this airport. As a matter of fact it is not operated any longer by the government, but was leased to the town of Virden, I do not know under whose jurisdiction. I am informed it is now used by a flying club.
The situation is this. Here is the government of this country that obtained this property for the purpose of using it in the war effort and with no thought in mind at all of gaining anything other than the use of the surface of that land. The government did not have in mind gaining the mineral rights in that property, and the government admits even now that it had no such thought in mind. It so happens that the government obtained valuable mineral property from an immigrant who could not read or write, and now the government turns around and uses a technical argument to say that Mr. Fontana has no claim.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Shame.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The reason I mention this is because it is not so long ago-only a year ago, in fact-that I had occasion, as did other hon. members, to raise the question of certain tax remissions made to certain corporations in the province of Quebec which involved several million dollars.
The minister raised the question, as did some of his legal supporters on his side of the house, that after all the Fontana case went to the supreme court and the court ruled that Mr. Fontana had no possibility of a claim. The matter I have just mentioned also went to the Exchequer Court of Canada, and the exchequer court ruled quite clearly that these corporations were liable for the taxation that had been imposed on them. They were ordered to pay and they did so. What did this government do then? It turned around and refunded half the money to the corporations after the exchequer court ruled in favour of the crown. It did that under the Financial Administration Act, which permits the government to do that if it is in the public interest.

On one or two occasions the Minister of National Revenue attempted to prove that the government was justified in doing this and that it was done in the public interest. He never did prove this to my satisfaction nor to the satisfaction, I think, of the taxpayers of this country; but this is an indication of the difference between the way in which the government leans over backwards to accommodate these huge corporations which are in a position to finance the Liberal party during elections, as compared with the attitude the government adopts toward a private individual, in this case a man who did not even have the advantage of education. He came here to Canada as an immigrant and served the interests of this country, and because of an inadvertence the government has obtained certain valuable property which they neither sought to obtain nor expected to get. In effect they received an unearned increment which they are not willing to share with this individual.
It has been said before that in this country there is one law for the rich and one law for the poor, and certainly the actions of the government in these two cases has done a great deal to confirm that view. I think the government would be well advised if instead of using these legal arguments and technicalities they took the humane view and shared this wealth which has been discovered with this poor man who parted with it through inadvertence, or through a technical error on the part of his legal counsel. In that way the government would indicate that they are willing to lend an ear and open their minds and hearts to the poor individual as well as the large corporations in this country.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, to come back to the item we were discussing a little while ago, the question of sovereignty over the northern areas, the minister indicated that Canada has not been a supporter of the sector theory. Would he explain to us what the attitude would be in the case of new lands which might be discovered north of these islands by another nation as a result of its explorations?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I have explained the reasons for the lines which have appeared on the maps of Canada since 1903. The claim is made to all discovered or undiscovered land which exists within those lines drawn on Canadian maps. I am assured by my deputy minister, who is quite an expert in territorial waters and waters generally, that there are no new lands to be discovered.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Are
we to assume from this that Canada makes no claim whatsoever to the waters in that
Supply-Northern Affairs area or to a measure of sovereignty and control over those waters?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
We claim our territorial
waters.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am
not going to document this at great length, although it could be done very appropriately. I would point out to the minister at this time that he is putting forth a most dangerous proposition. This publication by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys points out:
-the presence of the sector boundaries on official maps almost implies a claim to the "high seas" forming part of the Arctic ocean, over which it has always been presumed that it is impossible for national sovereignty to exist.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Should not this matter be dealt with by the Department of External Affairs rather than this department?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Quite right.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is all right; I do not quarrel with that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
This publication of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys definitely suggests the presumption that by drawing these lines these rights exist. Then at page 48 reference is made to Senator Poirier's sector. He was the man who first expounded the sector theory. I quote:
Senator Poirier's "sector", therefore, still remains in an indefinite official state, but it has recently come to take on added meaning with the possibility that large areas of sea ice may be used as airfields. If this becomes a reality, then the question of sovereignty over the ice in "Poirier's sector" will no doubt have to be examined, for it will have some of the aspects and uses of dry land.
With the time at our disposal it is regrettable that we cannot really hammer out this thing, because it is in the interests of Canada and the national defence of Canada. The minister's assumption that any country can come in and establish air bases and other defence efforts immediately north of Canada and south of the north pole flows directly-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I did not admit anything; I gave the legal position.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is one of the most dangerous propositions that has been expounded in this house for a long time.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You do not know what you are talking about.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The minister casts doubt on the assertion I made some time ago that we had never made any claim to this northern sector.

Supply-Northern Affairs Mr. Lesage: To the water and ice in the sector.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
At page 43 of this same publication put out by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys we find this: The polar claims do not appear to have been officially stated in public until June 1925, when the minister of the interior stated, on several occasions, during debates in the House of Commons, that Canada claimed "right up to the pole" (44a, pp. 3773, 4069, 4083). He also defined the longitudinal limits of the claim and tabled a map showing its extent.	In December 1953, the Prime
Minister of Canada reiterated the claim during House of Commons debate when he said:
"We must leave no doubt of our active occupation and exercise of our sovereignty in these northern lands right up to the pole."
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, just before we took recess I had been quoting from memoir 2, Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, geographical branch, on the boundaries of Canada and its provinces. I was just on the point of quoting what our present Prime Minister said, which was as follows:
We must leave no doubt of our active occupation and exercise of our sovereignty in these northern lands-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Lands.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: -right up to the pole.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Lands.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The minister is trying to emphasize "lands". I emphasize "right up to the pole". Nobody knows yet whether it is land or floating ice in the vicinity of the pole. I hope the minister will not dispute that. The publication continues:
Lines delimiting the sector have subsequently appeared on political maps of Canada published by the federal government.
This goes to the point that the minister has been trying to make as to why these lines have appeared showing our sovereignty extending right up to the pole.
These it is presumed, however, should merely be regarded as lines of allocation, which are delimited through the high seas or unexplored areas for the purpose of allocating lands without conveying sovereignty over the high seas.
I will not read again the subsequent passages read by the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace, but they indicate the fact that there was in existence in Canada for many years what we might call a sector

psychology in regard to this area to the north of Canada, and that everything in this sector running up to the north pole was looked upon as under Canadian sovereignty.
I do not want to enter into any further controversy with the minister over whether these ice masses are floating, anchored or high seas, but I would say that nobody knows whether there is or is not land there. Nobody knows how much of this ice is anchored on land and how much is floating. In any event, I think the minister has followed a completely contrary line to that which has been followed by successive governments in Canada probably from 1903 on but definitely from 1926 on, when the minister of the interior in effect claimed all these areas for Canada, and in going contrary to that position I think he has done a great disservice to the country by what you might call foreclosing any claim we might have to that area.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Make it short.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
-my minister in front of me is giving me some advice to make this as short as possible, but I really do not need too much advice from over there. But since I may get the credit or the blame for starting this, I should like to say simply this in conclusion. I do not take any credit as an international law authority; therefore I was not too much taken back this afternoon by the minister's remarks, but I should like to add this to what the hon. member for Calgary North has said. I think what constitutes a land mass, an ice mass or what are territorial waters in a sea area, is over and above any argument on the basis of legal principle. What we are stressing now is that changing conditions may necessitate a new outlook and a new statement of principle.
The minister has said that nobody will recognize it. There was an article in The Economist of Britain indicating that Russia had asserted the sector principle. It is true that they have named these floating islands, if that is what you want to call them. They have given them numbers, S.P.l, 2, 3 and 4, and as they disappear they go on with the numbering, 5, 6 and 7. As I understand it, these islands are on their side of the pole and are within their sector. But they have been using them for purposes of scientific research. I do not want to give the minister the opportunity of quoting all the authorities he has, but I would respectfully suggest in closing that the minister should have another look at the situation with respect to whether a new principle should be enunciated before it is too late.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when I
spoke yesterday on the general item I posed several questions with regard to northern administration, and I should like the minister to answer them now. One had to do with what steps the government is prepared to take, if any, in order to ensure continued Canadian control, particularly as far as civil powers and rights are concerned, in the northern areas where the D.E.W. line stations are now established. Another was in connection with transportation to the northern areas. I will not take the time to repeat exactly what the questions were. Perhaps the minister has made a note of them and can reply.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: As far as sovereignty is concerned, I dealt with that this afternoon in the course of my remarks which were prompted by the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary North and the hon. member for York West. I said, and I repeat tonight, that there has never been and there cannot be any questions as to our sovereignty on the continent and in the Arctic islands.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: If I may interject, it is not a matter of sovereignty. It is a matter of ensuring that Canadian civil rights and civil law are in operation and effect at all these northern D.E.W. stations.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I do not have with me the agreements which were signed between Canada and the United States and which were tabled at the last session. They are pretty voluminous documents. They guarantee that Canadian civil laws apply, that the area is under Canadian control, that our native population up north will be employed and protected, that our natural resources, including wildlife, will be protected. These things are all in the agreements and we have had no trouble at all with the United States authorities. Canadian law is applied according to the agreements and it has been applied in fact. There is no United States control on the D.E.W. line area.
I have visited the D.E.W. line myself. I accompanied the Minister of Defence Production and the Minister of National Defence on a visit to some of the stations. There is no doubt that Canadian sovereignty and control are recognized all along the line. Let us not forget that over 80 per cent of the people to be found at these stations are Canadian. They come from the various provinces and there are also Canadian Eskimos, who are Canadians with full citizenship rights. There are also a few Indians working in the Mackenzie delta at the present time.
The stations will be manned, maintained and operated under the direction of the
Supply-Northern Affairs Federal Electric Company, but arrangements are being made so that most of the employees for the maintenance and the operation of the D.E.W. line will be Canadians. I am glad and proud to say that the discussions we have had with the Federal Electric Company have been very successful from the point of view of providing as much employment as possible for our Eskimos in the north. There has been no difficulty. There has been some doubt cast about sovereignty or control. I am not referring to the hon. member for Calgary North because he has asked questions and has not made assertions, but I am afraid some people have asserted that Canadian control is not effective along the D.E.W. line. To use an expression used by the hon. member for Calgary North, these people have built a straw man and they have been trying to destroy it in their papers.
Nothing exists which one could call United States control in the north. It is Canadian control. Our northern service officers are constantly touring the line. The R.C.M.P. are constantly touring the line looking after order, peace and good behaviour on the part of everyone concerned. It is clear that Canadian law is applied and enforced, and that the control is in the hands of Canadians.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Before the minister goes on to the transport end of it, I think perhaps I should say that in my opinion he is begging the question. He started out by saying that certain agreements were made with the United States and that that covered the whole question. I do not think that covers the question at all, and it is directly contrary to the reports we have received from Canadian newspapermen who were on the trip through the north.
I think the main point I made was this. While there was no overt claim about sovereignty or anything along that line, in effect Canadian sovereignty and control of that area was not being excercised. In other words there were no Canadian civil authority officers at a considerable number of the D.E.W. line stations. As a matter of fact these particular newspapermen who went up there had to go down to New York, report to the United States authorities, and get clearance from the New York authorities, and as far as Canada was concerned she had nothing to do with it at all. All the security arrangements and everything else in connection with the matter or in connection with this particular trip were in the hands of the United States authorities. Possibly the minister is obliged to get authority from Washington before he can make a trip around those stations. I do not know whether that is so. That may be the situation. In any event, as

Supply-Northern Affairs far as Canadian custom regulations are concerned and everything along that line, that sort of thing just had no application whatever.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Oh, yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The point I made when I spoke yesterday was that we should have officers of this department or of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police at all these stations so that Canadian civil authorities are always in evidence, always apparent and always recognized.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Even during the construction of the D.E.W. line our northern service officers have been touring the line constantly. Moreover, to hear the hon. member talk one would think that the contractors up there were all United States contractors, whereas the fact is, as we know, that in connection with half the line-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: All of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: -the contract for the construction of half of the line, the western half of it, was given to Northern Construction Company and that for the construction of the eastern half of the line to Foundation Company of Canada, which are two Canadian companies.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I will say this finally in connection with this matter. I have not been up there. I do not know, to my personal knowledge, what the situation is. But all the Canadian newspapermen who went up there told stories about it and gave reports. The stories they wrote were more or less unanimously to the effect that Canadian control of the area had practically disappeared. As a matter of fact Ralph Allen said, "do the Canadians here resent the Americans and the American control of affairs?" and the man replied sadly: "It is exactly the other way around. The Americans resent their being here".

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Only two or three newspapermen have written stories in the sense just mentioned by the hon. member, out of a total of 20. The balance have not said anything like that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in the newspaper stories I have seen, all the people who went up there indicated that.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You saw the ones you wanted to see for the purpose of discussion of the estimates.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No; I read everything on these things that I can find. As I say, the stories in the papers and magazines have all been along the lines I have indicated.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Carried.
[Mr. Harkness.)

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES

speechtext:
My remarks will be very brief because I realize that we want to get through the estimates. This is an extremely important branch. I am pleased to know that there is an increase of something over $26,000 in the estimates of this branch. I think that is a very good sign. I am sorry to see a decrease in the item connected with the grant for forest inventory. I hope that does not indicate that the department is gradually going to back out of that field, because in my opinion forest inventory must be a continuing inventory if it is going to be worthwhile and of value to the persons concerned.
I am just going to mention two things.
I want to mention briefly a point I tried to make on a previous occasion, that in my opinion, and in the opinion of a large number of the people I represent, particularly those interested in the lumber industry, the most vital thing this government could do to assist in the protection of our forests at the present time would be to consider making grants to provincial governments toward forest fire protection. Just yesterday in the Kootenays there were 2,000 acres of timber burned within 24 hours. That is a tremendous loss. Yesterday in my own district of the Arrow lakes there were 15 fires started within one hour by lightning. This large number of fires commencing at once in one area create very serious problems for the the forest service. You have to have equipment to cope with that satisfactorily; you have to have men, and that means money.
I do make an appeal for the consideration of grants to the provinces for the improvement of forest fire protection.
In that connection I am just going to quote very briefly from this very excellent booklet published this year by the forestry branch of the minister's department and entitled "Research Work of the Forestry Branch." I had intended to say a bit more if we had not been cruising around the Arctic for quite so long. I am just going to quote this paragraph, "Forest fire protection section".
The chief natural enemy of the forests of Canada is fire. This statement is confirmed by the fact that about 50 per cent of the total expenditures by provincial forestry departments are incurred in connection with fire protection. Although great

Supply-Northern Affairs advances have been made in the development of fire protection services during the past 30 years, the danger that investments in forest improvements may literally go up in smoke continues to be a major deterrent to the development of sound forest management.
Those are very true words indeed. It is because of the fear of the loss of forests and of the investment in timber by fire that some companies and some governments still fail to practice the forest management policies that they should be practising at this stage.
The research work of the forestry branch in this field seeks to provide new information and to give assistance in the development of better methods which are essential to the further improvement of fire protection.
I give the branch credit for what it has been doing in this connection. This booklet mentions the very excellent work that is being done. Again I say I think the federal government could well reinvest part of the large sum of money it receives in the form of taxes from the forest industry in grants to the provinces for fire protection purposes. The same conclusions were reached at the conference held at the Chauteau Laurier in 1954 on renewable natural resources. I am not going to read the paragraph, but there again a request is made for some consideration by this government of grants to the provinces for this purpose.
Having said that, I want to mention one other matter. I think the branch does excellent research work, but I plead again for a wider distribution, if possible, of the literature the branch publishes. I know that every effort is being made to get this information into the hands of the people who will appreciate it; but within the last month I have had correspondence, for instance, from the mill manager of a company in which I am interested and the forestry engineer of the same company, asking for information on this and that. I know they have been pleased to receive many of these pamphlets and bulletins that I have sent. In my travels around the constituency I run into a number of lumbermen who operate on a small scale who are not aware of this information.
I do suggest that either through the lumbermen's association of British Columbia, the interior association or the other associations, a greater effort be made to get this excellent information, resulting from research on the part of this branch, into the hands of the men who are producing logs and manufacturing lumber in this country.
Now I want to make one suggestion in :espect of research. I have been very interested for some years in fire-resistant paints and things of that sort for wood. I made some inquiries of the national research council and found they had not carried on (Mr. Herridge.l
any research or investigations in that respect. They had dealt with private companies. I think they do give information as to those who are dealing with this matter, and I understand they consider it best to leave research in this field to the private companies in Canada.
I understand this branch has done some work in this respect. This is a type of research that I hope the research branch of the forestry branch will carry on extensively, because it offers a great opportunity. I have heard the question discussed amongst lumbering people and people who want to use our splendid cedar, fir and other woods for roofing and interior and exterior finishing.
I understand that in the United States considerable work has been done along this line.
I know of people who desire to use wood not because of the cheapness but because it is a long lasting type of roof. I might mention that regardless of what the manufactured roofing might be, asbestos or whatever it is, according to the Washington department of documents the cedar shake roof is the most efficient and longest lasting, and in the long run the cheapest roof you can put on at the present time. The same is true of the red cedar shingles of British Columbia.
I suggest this is a problem worthy of the very close attention of our forestry branch, because if we get some solution for the protection of wood by coating it with paints or other commodities that will reduce the fire hazard, we will have accomplished a very important thing for the lumber industry as a whole and for those persons in Canada who prefer to use Canadian woods in building and beautifying their homes, rather than these synthetic materials that are foisted on people today because they are in some cases, under present circumstances, the most easily available and more fire-resistant.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
It seems to me that the service to forestry development in this country by the dominion government has been sadly neglected for many years. It is not a case of political differences with any one party, but there seems to be a lack of understanding as to the part that forestry plays in our whole economy.
The hon. member for Royal has mentioned the budworm. We know very well from historical facts that down through the years since 1850-in fact again in 1875, and again later on-we have had these budworm infestations. I do not want to hold up the estimates, because I would like to see this house prorogue; but I feel that this is one very important factor of which the government should take more cognizance. It is not a matter of political differences; it is just a matter of lack of appreciation. From no industry in Canada does the government receive so much income tax and so much benefit as from the pulp and paper industry.
We hear a great deal about the conservation of our resources and of this government not preserving those great natural resources, and I hear a lot of people talking about what has been done to those forests by cutting down the trees. Yet the same people will probably throw half-burned cigarettes in a forest district and do more harm than all the harm they have been talking about that others have done to the forests of this country.
I sometimes think that people have a misconception of our forests. Our forests are like crops. Trees grow as people do. They develop, ripen and mature and become overripe and ready for harvesting. You would not take a wheat field and say to the farmer, "You should not cut that golden field of wheat because it is so beautiful. You are ravaging the agricultural soil by cutting the wheat. It is the same with spruce, balsam and poplar and any trees that are ready to cut and be developed into resources and put into our economy to give employment to our people. It is a crop.
I do say this, Mr. Chairman, and I can say it now, as you probably know, with better grace than I could have some time ago,

Supply-Northern Affairs because I am not connected with any pulp and paper industry in Canada in any managerial or executive position. I do say, independent of politics, that the government of Canada should stop, look and listen with respect to the development of our great resources. I have been a farmer all my life, and I have urged that expenditures be made on agriculture. We have expenditures on agriculture in western and eastern Canada, but no industry in Canada has contributed so much to the national economy and received so little from the Ottawa government as the forestry industry. I take part of the blame myself. It is not a condemnation of the present government; it is the attitude of the government at Ottawa, irrespective of what party is in power.
The budworm infestation, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce knows probably better than most members in the house-I think he will agree with me in this-destroyed probably 10 million cords in the district with which he and I are so familiar.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The lake Nipigon area alone.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Yes, in the lake Nipigon area alone, 10 million cords. I think he will agree that this industry has returned to the treasury of the dominion tremendous amounts in income tax and so on. We return enormous sums to agriculture, the basic industry, as it is called, of this country, which many of us are interested in; but the pulp and paper industry is criticized for having ravaged the forests." I think the minister will agree with me that from Newfoundland right out to the far west coast, which several hon. members to my left know so well, the companies have tried to play the game. They have tried to establish protection for the forests; they have tried to establish reforestation. The provinces have helped some, but the provinces have not given as much as they might have done, and I think the dominion government should take a new look at what could be done.
We talk about the trans-Canada highway. We need highways through the forests. Don't let us charge the tourists with having thrown out cigarette butts and started fires. The good Lord and nature with lightning start far more fires than anything else. It is almost impossible, either by helicopter or plane, to get into many of those areas. There is nothing that would help more than highways through those areas, and a great deal could be done along that line.
I urge the minister to try to get the members of the cabinet to take a new look at this great resource because, after all, we stand out as the greatest country in the world

so far as pulp and paper and timber resources are concerned. During the years of the 1930's, in those awful years, the gold of this country and our forest resources were the key links keeping this country going.
As the hon. member for Royal has so well said, the budworm infestation is terrific. You hear people saying, those who probably have not studied the issue very carefully, that the pulp and paper industry and the lumbermen are stripping the forests and cutting down the beautiful trees and not planting anything else. But keep in mind that the whole pulp and paper industry in Canada consumes only a little more than 25 per cent of the annual depletion of our forests, while fire alone takes almost 25 per cent. The firewood to keep houses warm in districts that have no coal or oil takes almost another 25 per cent.
It seems to me that we are often carried away by the idea that 10 million, 12 million or 13 million cords of wood are cut to keep the pulp and paper industry and the lumber industry going, which bring in about $1,500 million a year in our balance of trade; yet we hear-and I am not critical of this in a political sense-that about $3 million will be spent to protect this. I have urged before in the house and I urge at this time that the government take another look at what could be done to help perpetuate this great resource. The only difference between a crop of golden wheat and a crop of black spruce is that it takes about 60 years to grow a crop of black spruce and something less than six months to grow a crop of wheat. They both must be harvested in time; there shall be a time for seeding and a time for harvesting.
The hon. member for Fort William and others who have lived in the north country know that what I say is true. If a forest is properly harvested it is not depleted, and just because you cut down a beautiful tree it does not mean that another one will not grow in its place; it simply means that perhaps you and I may not be here to see it.
The budworm infestation has been the tragedy of the forest over the last 75 years. The infestation came over from the state of Maine into New Brunswick and Nova Scotia probably 80 years ago, and then it moved on down into Ontario. It has been most devastating, and I know it is almost impossible to eradicate. In the province of Ontario the budworm was sprayed from aeroplanes and various other measures were taken to kill the budworms; but they moved out into the lakes and killed the fish, and there were all sorts of repercussions along the line.
I do believe that the dominion government should be more active in co-operating with the various provinces across Canada in an

effort to defeat the budworm. It must be remembered that the budworm does not understand or acknowledge provincial boundaries. I realize that this matter is a provincial responsibility, but I think it is a matter the importance of which we in this chamber fail to emphasize in relation to our whole national economy.
For instance, let us think of our fire protection system. A fire could start in the province of Quebec and sweep through the province of Ontario. Forest fires disrespect provincial borders; we have seen them do that. I feel there should be closer co-operation between the federal and provincial governments. As a matter of fact I think the provinces should co-operate more in building highways through the various forest areas, and I think the federal government should be as interested in developing such roadways as it is in building the trans-Canada highway.
Another aspect of this matter I have mentioned once before in this house and would like to bring up again at this time is that if we should ever become involved in another tragic war-and God forbid that it should ever happen-we should try to conceive what might happen in view of the development of these disastrous and terrible instruments of destruction that could destroy our national wealth very quickly if two or three bombs fell in our forests during a dry season in the summer. If this should ever happen the highways I have referred to would be extremely important.
I am not going to delay the house because I am anxious to see this session expedited and concluded, but I urge upon the minister to talk to his colleagues, especially the Minister of Trade and Commerce, for he knows as I do that what I have said is true. Let us look at this squarely, independently of parties, as an issue that involves one of the greatest resources of this country, and let us give some consideration to doubling, trebling and possibly quadrupling the money that is spent for our forest development and protection.
Personally I would like to see some arrangement made whereby we would have highways built through these forest areas, areas that are not yet taken up by any company, so that in case of fire, budworm infestation or enemy attack we would have ways and means of reaching those districts and safeguarding one of the greatest resources we have. No other people in the world have ever had a single resource such as we Canadians have. We have the greatest forest resources in the world. Canada is now
Supply-Northern Affairs supplying 85 per cent of the world's newsprint, almost all of it, and about 65 per cent of the world's pulp. This is a resource that is worth as much as gold itself. I can speak in this way because at the moment I am not identified with any company.
As a member of this house I feel that we in this chamber have not fully comprehended the importance of this vital resource, and independently of our party affiliations we have not quite done all that we should do to safeguard and protect it. As a farmer I do not mind if the government spends $12 million, $18 million or $100 million in subsidies for agriculture, but I shudder to think that in relation to this great resource which returns so much to the federal treasury we on both sides of the house appear to consider it as picayune and are adopting an attitude of reckless abandon.

A great deal has been said by the ministry of fisheries in connection with this matter.
The people in New Brunswick are very much concerned to know whether there has been any great lack of responsibility on the part of any of the parties concerned in connection with the destruction of certain fisheries in our province. I thought perhaps the minister might be able to enlighten us on this particular matter.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was concerned with a question asked by the Leader of the Opposition on July 20 of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources regarding the spruce budworm outbreak in the Cape Breton highland national park area around Ingonish beach.
I had the pleasure of spending a few days in the Cape Breton highland national park and I visited that area two or three days before the question was raised in the house. I was concerned about the minister's reply when he said that he had obtained a report from the forest biology division of the Department of Agriculture to the effect that there was no real, sudden outburst. There may have been some infestation in the national park, but there was nothing extraordinary. After you drive into the park for a bit you find an area which was burned over seven years ago, and that certainly is not a beautiful sight for tourists. An area of burned bare trees cannot be considered a tourist attraction.
I am concerned that in the Ingonish area there has been a serious outbreak of the spruce budworm. Wherever you look you see nothing green; the new growth has been completely devoured. If you walk into the trees in a few moments you are completely covered with grubs. I would hate to see that beautiful park area devoured. Cape Breton national park is one of the outstanding parks in eastern Canada, and with the improvements being made on the road it should be a real tourist attraction. I wonder if the minister has any comments to make.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am informed that there has been an outbreak, although not too serious. This is not confined to the park area


but covers that part of the province. Our technical people are studying the matter along with the officials of the forest biology division of the Department of Agriculture, and there will also be talks with the appropriate officials of the provincial government to see what can be done.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Is any spraying being done at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I will have to get a report from the technical people before I can make a decision that spraying should be done. I am not an expert, but I understand that spraying must be done in June if it is to be effective, because that is the only time you can kill the budworm. The hon. member for Royal nods his head. If any decision is taken as to what can be done and if it involved spraying would have to wait until next June.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this item which deals with the Canadian government travel bureau is important to all Canada, because travel in this country by people from the United States or other parts of the world represents one of our major sources of foreign exchange. In recent years, while there has seemed to be an improvement in our travel position, the actual case is that we have been falling back rather badly in the number of people who come to Canada as tourists. The best basis of comparison which can be offered is the expenditures of United States citizens for travel in other countries. I intend to compare 1948 with 1954.
We find that in 1948 United States citizens expended about 21 per cent of their travel expenditures in Europe. This has increased to 38 per cent. In 1948 they spent 19 per cent in Mexico; today they are spending about the same, 20 per cent. In the case of Canada we find that their expenditures in 1948 represented 44 per cent of the total, but those expenditures had dropped to 30 per cent in 1954. That is clear and conclusive and definite evidence that the Canadian government travel bureau is not doing the job it should or which it could do to attract the citizens of other countries to Canada to spend their time and money in this country.
This tremendous dropping off in the proportion of United States travel funds spent in Canada is masked by the fact that their dollar expenditures have gone up, but the fact remains that we have been getting a smaller and smaller share of that amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am delighted to have the minister bring up that point. That is why I deliberately chose the year 1948. By 1948 the war had been over for several years. Transportation to Europe-

speechtext:
Hotels had been renovated. One of the great attractions in Europe at that particular time was the exchange situation, which was very heavily in favour of the United States traveller going to Europe. Despite all these advantages, in that year we were still able to attract 44 per cent of the total United States dollar expenditures on travel, but by 1954 that percentage had fallen to 30 per cent. I am delighted that the minister gave me the opportunity to emphasize that point.
As I have said, these statistics would seem to indicate that the department has been doing an unsatisfactory job in this field. I suggest also that in the coming years travel will be of increasing importance as a source of foreign exchange to a country like ours, which needs it so badly. With automation, the reduction of the work week and a higher standard of living, more and more dollars are going to flow into travel expenditures, and we must be prepared to get our share. Therefore if our attractions for the tourist or our way of merchandising them are unsatisfactory now, it betokens a condition which will become increasingly serious in the future.
Having said that, I should like to proceed to a few points that might be of some assistance to the minister in dealing with this problem. The first suggestion I would make is that the responsibility for the travel bureau be transferred from the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources to the Department of Trade and Commerce. Travel is not a natural resource. It is a trade; it is something which has to be merchandised and sold. In the foreign countries of this world we already have a magnificent organization of Canadian government trade commissioners. They can do an excellent job of handling tourist promotion in

Supply-Northern Affairs those areas. While we are taking advantage of their services to a very limited extent at the present time, there is no co-ordination and no integration. Therefore I suggest the transfer of this branch of the government to a department where it would be genuinely at home.
Because on occasion I have been known as a critic of the Minister of Trade and Commerce for having too much to do and too much under his control, I suggest in passing that he trade to the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources the Eldorado Mining and Refining operation in return for the Canadian government travel bureau, for I can realize that nobody likes to lose part of his empire without getting a little bit from somebody else. The Northern Transportation Company, which is closely allied with Eldorado Mining and Refining, might also go along to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, or it might find its way into the Department of Transport.
However, while that suggestion would deal at least in part with improving the merchandising of Canada's tourist attractions, it would not deal with one of the biggest oversights in the work of the bureau at the present time. I refer to its complete concentration upon selling Canada and travel in Canada to other nations and in the process overlooking completely the possibilities involved in Canadians travelling from one part of Canada to another and becoming better acquainted with their own country.
The reason I bring that up at this point is that it does not matter whether we attract a United States dollar into this country to be spent by a tourist or whether we retain a Canadian dollar in this country rather than see it go south of the border to the United States. The net effect on our exchange position is exactly the same.
Therefore it would seem to me that by persuading some of the millions of Canadians who go to the United States each year to stay in Canada and see Canada our exchange position would be the same or better, and we would have a great rebirth of interest in this country. I would also point out that it would be of tremendous benefit to certain areas such as the maritimes, which are keenly interested in increasing their financial resources at the present time.
Turning from this point to the question of the extent to which the travel bureau is actually doing a job at this time, I wonder whether the house and the minister realize that a little country like Mexico, little in comparison to Canada, is spending approximately $4 million on the promotion of travel for its purposes as against $1,500,000 by us, or almost


three times as much as Canada. A few minutes ago I quoted figures which showed the effect of that expenditure. From 1948 to 1954, while expenditures by Americans on travel in Canada dropped from 44 per cent to 30 per cent, expenditures by Americans in Mexico remained almost static. They were 19 per cent of the total expenditure in 1948 and 20 per cent in 1954. That is very directly the result of proper and adequate merchandising by Mexico.
I would point out to the minister that little places like the Bahama islands and Bermuda, places with not a hundredth or a thousandth of the resources of Canada, surpass our budget in their expenditures on tourist promotion for their countries.
In some respects the work of the tourist bureau is very attractive. I hold in my hand their booklet called "Canada, Vacations Unlimited". It is an attractive piece, well printed and well done; but if the minister will consult with advertising experts or experts on tourism I think he will find that most of the bureau's promotional literature, including "Canada, Vacations Unlimited", has missed one of the main points of tourist promotion, the need for regional promotion, to make a thing come alive in terms that the person reading it can understand.
This booklet first of all promotes Canada as a whole; and while that is a good thing, it is something which it is difficult to sell. Next it promotes features of tourism in Canada such as adventure in the wilderness, scenic transportation, fun and games. You can have fun and games in any country in the world. Certainly that is no special feature which is going to draw people to this country. Then there is reference to national parks. We have very attractive national parks. So has the United States. The booklet refers to shrines and historic places in Canada. I shall deal with that in a moment but in general terms all countries have shrines and historic places. In other words this booklet and this expenditure is not showing with respect to Canada anything new or different which would have a special attraction for people outside our borders.
It then goes ahead to deal with the provinces, and that is a good thing, more under the basis of regional promotion; but it still does not make the reason come alive in the minds of the prospective tourists to Canada as to why they should come here rather than go somewhere else. I suggest to the minister that he would get immeasurably better results from his expenditures in this field if he would promote vividly very narrow regions, taking not a province but small areas in a province and showing much more specifically what the tourist will find.

I also suggest to the minister that far more emphasis should be placed by his department on the specific aspects of Canadian history which tie in so closely with the United States of America and with the European countries. We were the first settled country on the North American continent. We have a history which comes vividly alive in various parts of this country, as in Quebec city itself, Montreal, Kingston, the point where the first passage was made through the Rockies, and in a thousand and one places. There are in Canada for tourists tremendously exciting experiences which have never been promoted and have never been brought to their attention by the federal tourist bureau.
These suggestions will admittedly make many demands upon the budget of the tourist bureau. I am one of those who seldom rise in this house and advocate a specific additional expenditure. When I do so I like to feel that the expenditure which is being advocated is tied to a specific return to this country or to the federal government. I suggest to the minister that there are very few fields in which a dollar spent will bring a greater return to Canada than would be brought here through proper expenditures by the federal tourist bureau, expenditures which would be somewhere in line with or equal to those of a country like Mexico, whose resources are so much more limited than are ours, or an area like the Bahama islands or Bermuda, all of which are spending on their tourist promotion more than we are spending. I suggest to the minister that our limited promotion is at the very root of the reason we are enjoying or rather' suffering-that is a far better word-such a serious adverse balance of trade in respect of our tourist business.
There are many more things that could be said on this matter, Mr. Chairman, but it seems to me that I have put quite a few ideas forward, and at least I have drawn the minister's attention to the matter. In deference to his wish to get through his estimates as quickly as possible I shall now await his reply on these matters.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a few minutes of the time of the committee in order to record a few facts which are of vast importance to my own province and which I think perhaps might be of great importance to people in other parts of Canada and elsewhere.
I have in my hand the issue of the Charlottetown Guardian of July 10, in which is reported an interview with Dr. Elzear Cam-pagna who is recognized as an expert on ragweed. In the interview he is reported as follows:
"You have a gold mine here on Prince Edward Island and you don't know it," said Dr. Elzear
Supply-Northern Affairs Campagna of the faculty of agriculture at Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere, Quebec, yesterday who has pioneered in the eradication of ragweed in eastern Canada since 1936.
The article continues further:
From surveys which he started in 1936, he has found that Prince Edward Island is one the the areas most free of ragweed which is one of the main causes of hayfever. Dr. Campagna states that the hayfever season is from the 15th of August to the 15th of September and if Island conditions are sufficiently advertised this province could easily become a mecca for sufferers from the affliction. These people could be, as it were, a "second harvest" to the regular tourist business which is pretty well over at this time of year.
Dr. Campagna notes that many sufferers from hayfever spend large amounts of money trying to find relief from the affliction and only a small percentage of these have been successful. "It would be much cheaper and a great deal more pleasant for them to come to a place which is free from affliction such as your province," he said.
In case it might be of some value to places which are trying to eradicate this weed I might say that Dr. Campagna said that the eradication of the plant is not an expensive procedure. He says that about two ounces of 2-4D to a gallon of water will effectively destroy it. I might conclude by quoting the closing words of the interview:
In concluding his remarks, Dr. Campagna said: "You have something here which is even more valuable than gold-gold may be mined and sold and you do not possess it any more-but an area which is free of ragweed is a constant source of income to its people."

Would consideration be
given to assistance in cases where it is considered advisable that temperature controls be installed in those warehouses to keep the temperature down in hot weather so that potatoes can be stored in good condition near the point of production, rather than necessarily in the large cities during the hot weather in the summer?
