maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am wondering whether the minister has given any consideration at all to equalizing support prices on hogs across Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Yes, we have given consideration to it, but we give that consideration having in mind the many applications that have been made in an attempt to equalize freight rates across Canada, and it would be very difficult to apply it to one product without applying it to others. One need only say that to realize the enormous amount of money that would be involved if we attempted to do any such thing in the movement of products generally across the country.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
I am
prepared to go quite a way with the minister on this, when one considers the pressure that is on us at the present time; but I do think that the hog producers of the province of Alberta are being called upon to face a situation which they should not have to face. For example, in the city of Edmonton the floor price for hogs is $18.50. Ninety per cent of the hogs that are exported from the province of Alberta go to the British Columbia market. It only costs $1 a hundred to move them out. I think the hog producers in the province of Alberta are actually being called upon to
Supply-Agriculture
do something they should not have to do. Someone is making something on this.
In closing my remarks I urge the minister and his department to give serious consideration to trying to do something in the way of equalizing the support price on hogs throughout all of Canada within the next year.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: As I said, Mr. Chairman, we have been giving consideration to the matter and we are inclined to think that probably Alberta is better off than any province. They are not far removed from the Vancouver market and their hogs can get there at a comparatively low freight rate. The price, too, is generally favourable on the coast. If we were to do what the hon. member asked, we would have to consider paying the freight on a much greater number of hogs that go down to the eastern market.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: From Alberta?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: No, from Saskatchewan and Manitoba. We deal, of course, with hog producers right across Canada, and provincial boundaries do not count in that kind of thing. As my hon. friend has said, over 90 per cent of the hogs move from Alberta to Vancouver, which is a relatively short distance; and few hogs, say 10 per cent, move from Alberta east. Practically all the hogs that are moved fi'om Saskatchewan and Manitoba are moved to the east. I can assure the hon. member that freight costs on those hogs would be very much higher. If we tried to equalize out in Alberta we would be expected to equalize in the other provinces as well.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I hope the minister will take this under advisement and study the problem, because I cannot yet see any justification for a floor price of $23 a hundredweight at Toronto and Montreal for the hog producers in Ontario, and the floor price of only $18.50 for the hog producers in Alberta. I shall drop it at this point.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Would the minister give us some idea why this inequitable disparity should prevail?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: The disparity may prevail on the floor price but not on the price the farmer receives for hogs in Alberta as compared with the price received in other provinces. The price in Alberta is considerably more above the floor than is the case in the other western provinces.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I cannot accept that, and I must

Supply-Agriculture
state that is a very debatable point. However, we shall continue with this discussion at another time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, could the minister give some figures to justify the remark he has just made? We in Alberta do not feel satisfied about this matter. Could the minister give actual figures, for example, for the month of February or January at Alberta points and at Manitoba points? What the minister says is not in accordance with the information we have.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
I am sorry, but I do not have the prices here. I have them on my desk over in my office. They come in every morning and are put on my desk. I do not check them every morning but I check them throughout the week, and we have studies made of them from time to time. I can assure my hon. friend, however, that the situation is as I have outlined it.
The hogs do sell on the western coast at a price that is at least as good as that which they obtain in other markets; this is true most of the time. The province of Alberta is able to take advantage of the Vancouver market. The market is too far away from Saskatchewan and Manitoba for the hog producers there to take advantage of it, and therefore any advantage there is in having that market goes to Alberta. I think that is generally understood by the trade.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I believe the minister will recognize the fact that much has been said about the amount of the subsidy that is paid to agriculture. According to the annual report of the department for the year ending March 31, 1955, the total amount paid at March 31, 1954 was some $80 million, of which the sum of $69 million was due to the foot-and-mouth epidemic in 1952, and this has to do with pork and beef. Another amount of $923,000 is charged up in the 1954-55 period and that brings the total to barely $1 million a year which has been spent on agricultural price supports not including beef and pork during the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease.
The sum of $2 million is put aside by the government each year for this purpose, and apparently the sum of only $1 million a year has been spent. I think no one could criticize that too much, and I hope the urban people realize how little is paid to agriculture as compared with the amount paid to other industries across this country that are nonagricultural.
I did not give the figures for the end of 1954. The last report of the agricultural prices support board gives figures including

the year ending March 31, 1955, and the sum of only $3 million more was spent in the 1954-55 period.
I think the minister should give some kind of statement concerning the amount of subsidy paid to the agricultural industry as compared to the amount paid to non-agricultural industries, because I am sure that coming from the minister this information would mean more than if it were to be given by an individual member of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, I
thought it was not going to be necessary for me to say anything, because I understood the hon. member to be speaking favourably of the amount that has been paid out. I only wish to state that the total amount paid out over the years beginning with 1946, which was the first year there were any payments under this, is $89,196,061.31. That includes the figure for the 1955-56 period, which is a year in addition to the years for which the hon. member has just given us the figures.
That sum is made up of an amount of $2,036,000 on potatoes. I will just give round figures in most cases. It also includes $6,700,000 on apples, $194,000 on dried beans, $177,000 on extracted honey, $677,000 on dried skim milk, $155,000 on Cheddar cheese, $8,542,378 on creamery butter, $673,194.39 on eggs, and on hogs, practically all of which came in the foot-and-mouth activities, $36,673,894.07. On cattle, again including the foot-and-mouth disease, it was $33,358,015.86, making a total of $89,196,061.31.
The fund is a revolving one in the amount of $200 million. We can, of course, utilize up to that amount each year to the extent that we get the money back into the fund again without drawing any more from the treasury. We simply draw from the treasury from time to time when it is necessary to do so and the sum of about $350 million has been utilized altogether. From year to year we get a certain percentage of it back into the fund from selling the products. There has only been a net amount spent of $89,196,061.31. That is the total for fighting foot-and-mouth disease and to carry on the other activities.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Outside of the foot-andmouth disease it would amount to about $1 million a year?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: The total is about $19 million now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Over the ten years that is the total?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, around May 3 I put on the record the actual cost of raising a hog from the weaning stage right up to the market stage, and I should like to ask the minister if during the coming year he will have one of his experimental farms make a careful survey of how much it actually costs to raise a hog to market stage. If the minister wishes he can do it on his own farm, taking everything into consideration except his own salary as cabinet minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: This has been done a number of times at the Guelph agricultural college, but I do not know whether it has been done in the last two or three years. It has been done at the university at Edmonton and at quite a number of places. I am afraid if farmers were to follow the course followed in setting up these figures there would not be many of us producing hogs. I do not think it is fair to say that if you do not meet all the conditions set out in these figures no farmer is going to make money out of producing hogs.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
The
minister has just asked me to spend a little longer on this. The farmers of Canada are not raising hogs to the extent they did last year, and I think the minister knows that as well as anyone else. I should like to quote from the Wheat Pool Budget of July 27, which contains the following hog forecast:
The number of hogs on Canadian farms as at June 1 was 61 per cent below the previous year's figure, reports the dominion bureau of statistics and a continuing downward trend is forecast. In western Canada the reduction was 11 per cent. A June 1 survey showed a Canadian total of 5,680,000 head compared to 6,075,000 a year ago.
This spring's pig crop amounted to 4,300,000 or 11 per cent less than the 1955 total. In the west the reduction was 14 per cent.
I do not wish to prolong this debate at all, but I submit to the minister that the reason for this is that the farmers in western Canada just cannot afford to raise hogs at the prices they are being paid.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Can the minister suggest an adequate reason why there should be that falling off in the production of hogs? I think in Alberta we have conditions which are probably as conducive to the production of hogs as can be found anywhere in the nation, so why should we have difficulty producing hogs?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
I think the other side of the picture ought to be given. The last time we had these estimates before the house we were complaining that the price of hogs was down to the floor; as a matter of fact we were afraid that they were going to go through the
Supply-Agriculture
floor. The price of hogs today and yesterday was about $29.50, or $6.50 per hundredweight above the floor.
This question has been discussed over a long period of time. If the number of hogs produced did go down very far it is due to the fact that the people who were in and out are out at the present time. Those of us who stayed in all the time have gained the advantage. The trouble with figuring on this basis as to whether a man makes money producing hogs is that there are many people like the fellow who tries to guess the time to get in and the time to get out. He has more difficulty; but those of us who go along producing hogs-and I may say for the benefit of my hon. friend that I have just as many sows as I had in the wartime, and so do nearly all the regular hog producers; they have not been in and out-are not in the position of those who went out at the end of the war.
That helped the fellow who went on producing hogs all the time because he had to. That is, they are making money. There are farms in certain parts of Canada which could not be run if they did not have hogs, but there are farms in other places where they can quit feeding hogs and produce something else.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
I do not
want to leave this without again asking the minister to make several surveys. I want to point out to him that the provincial cooperative association which has been in hogs for a number of years is not an in and out concern at all. I cannot accept the minister's argument at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: The total hog production is up 8-9 per cent, not down; those are the marketings of hogs. It is true that they are down in western Canada but they are up in eastern Canada. I think my hon. friend understands the reason for that. Most of us in western Canada would rather produce wheat than feed hogs. When we can make enough to get by with the wheat that is what we do. There are other times when we feed hogs.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: I certainly hope the minister is not under the impression that the wheat farmers of western Canada are in a position today where they can forgo the marketing of hogs because of the huge profits being made out of the marketing of wheat.

41. Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and water storage, $4,142,965.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Will the minister review the work which has been done in northern Manitoba and particularly in the interlake country by the federal and provincial governments in an effort to lower the lake levels? Two years ago a survey was started to see if anything could be done to lower the level of the lake because so many people were being drowned out. At that time it was thought the survey would take five years, and the dominion and provincial governments were each to pay $150,000 per year for the five years. When I discussed the matter with the minister some time ago he agreed to do some checking into the matter so he could give me some up to date information when his estimates came up. Perhaps the minister can indicate what the position is and if the agreement has been signed.
I am anxious to have this information because I told some people back home that the agreement between the dominion and provincial governments had already been made, under which the federal government would pay one-half and the provincial government the other half, with the work being done by the provincial government. I want to get myself clear with my constituents when I go back. I thought this had all been arranged but some time ago the minister told me that he was not quite sure and would make some inquiries.
While I am on my feet and to save time, there is another matter I should like to raise. It is in respect to the P.F.R.A. helping the provincial government to run a ditch from Rembrandt to meet the Drunken river and thence into lake Winnipeg to take care of a lot of water they have in that district. There seems to be a lot of surplus water there, and a fair sized ditch would be needed to bring it into the lake. It would help do away with flooding in that part of the country.
I am informed that the public works department of the provincial government has done some survey work in this part of the country from Rembrandt to Arnes and thence into the lake. The great problem, of course, is the cost. I am informed on good authority that the provincial government is prepared to pay half the cost if the dominion government will give some consideration to putting up the other half. In fact, I am informed that $15,000 was put in the Manitoba estimates for this work if the federal government would agree to pay the other half.
I want to appeal to the minister at this time to have the officers of his department look into this matter and see if it would be possible for the federal government to comply

with the request to have the ditch built to drain this part of the interlake country.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as a matter of fact we do not take the responsibility for drainage in any of the provinces. Even in the area that is under P.F.R.A. in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba we do not take the responsibility for drainage. That is considered to be a purely provincial matter, as in all the other provinces of Canada. The area between the lakes in Manitoba is not even under P.F.R.A. The boundary line, as my hon. friend knows, strikes the south end of lake Manitoba and then runs almost directly across to the Red river. The area south and west of that line is in the P.F.R.A. area. The works concerning which we have agreed to pay dollar for dollar with the province of Manitoba are over on the west side of lake Manitoba. Some of the streams drain into Dauphin lake and some into lake Manitoba.
But in those cases where we have gone out of the Assiniboine river drainage basin we have only gone there where the waters have their origin in the national park and flow out from the park on to some of the land. In those instances we have agreements with the Manitoba government under which we spend a certain amount. That has been going on for some years. In the year we are now in the amount being expended is $150,000, as was suggested. At the time we were discussing this before I was in the hope that we would have an agreement extending over three or five years, but that has not materialized. We have made agreements year by year, and last year's expenditure was $150,000. I presume this one will be about the same, and we may go on for some little time under that arrangement.
But, as was said, the Manitoba government carries out these works. We pay all the engineering cost and half the cost of the construction work that is done and our expenditure, as was suggested, is about $150,000. With respect to the other drainage in between, we have no part in that unless it be that the province asks us for some engineering help. We might do that, but we take no part otherwise.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: You would not look favourably on giving us a little money to help us to get that ditch?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: We do not.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: But would you look favourably on it?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: We will treat Manitoba exactly the same as we treat all other provinces. I will look that favourably upon it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: There should be something done there. If it could not be helped I would not make the request, but if a ditch is put in there it will drain that country and allow people to earn their own livelihood without coming to the minister and asking for assistance under P.F.A.A. It is only a matter of $15,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: This house has not voted me any authority to spend any money on drainage.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: I am asking for assistance and help, and I am asking you to let your department go a little bit farther north and do something about it. That is the work of the P.F.R.A.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: No, that is not a prairie farm rehabilitation area.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Then I do not know what it is. They are producing grain, and I think they have all the qualifications necessary to qualify.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: I wonder whether items 41 and 42 could stand. The hon. member for Assiniboia has some remarks to make but he is at another meeting. I could speak for half an hour, but I think it would facilitate the business if we allowed these items to stand and went on with the others.

45.	Land protection and reclamation; clearing and settlement of new lands under such terms and conditions as may be approved by the governor in council, $850,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Would the minister be good enough to give a further word of explanation in addition to what is in the details? I should like to know particularly where the money is chiefly being spent and under what conditions areas qualify for benefits under this item. Does it apply only to crown land or some scheme in which a provincial government is interested, or might it also apply to privately owned land in the case of a co-operative or a group of farmers?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
This amount is voted for special projects that may be in any of the provinces across Canada, and we only make expenditures where we have entered into agreements with the provinces. The northwestern escarpment region is the Riding-Duck mountain watershed which I was talking about a few moments ago. There is $150,000 for the watershed in the Porcupine
Supply-Agriculture
forest reserve. That is the amount in the estimates for that. Then there is the Saskatchewan river reclamation project in the Pasqua area. It is the Saskatchewan river but it is in Manitoba, and the amount for the work being done in the Pasqua area is $500,000. Then there is an unallotted amount of $200,000 covering situations that did not exist when this was drawn up. Of that amount $125,000 has been allotted to Newfoundland.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: What is the nature of the work being done on the Saskatchewan river? The minister said that $500,000 was being spent there. On what kind of work is that being spent?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: It is a project down toward the mouth of the Saskatchewan river in the province of Manitoba, where there is flooding in the spring of the year. When the water is high at any time of the year there is flooding. That is being diked very much in the same way that we diked lands in the maritime provinces to keep the ocean out. This is being diked to keep the river out. The Manitoba government asked us to do that work on their behalf. We do it and pay for it and then we are paid back from the sale of the lands in that area behind the dikes. I should say that 75 per cent of what the lands are sold for comes to us and only 25 per cent goes to the province. Over a period of years the greater part of it will be paid back.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: In many places we find that where a river makes a rather sharp bend it tends to cut into the bank and cause caving in of the soil above the cut. Has the minister any policy for taking care of situations like that? Sometimes a number of acres will fall right into the stream.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Again that is pretty much a provincial matter unless it is a navigable stream. The federal government does take action in connection with any matter of that kind, and even on the Assiniboine river not very far removed from these other works we have done diking and in some places we straighten out the stream. Where we straighten out the stream that is done because that stream has always been rated as a navigable stream and the work was originally carried out by the works department. Three or four years ago the vote was transferred to this department and the work is done under P.F.R.A. but it is the same type of work.
This particular piece at Pasqua is not that type. The whole province of Manitoba has been built from the old lake Aggasiz which constituted practically the whole area which

Supply-Agriculture
is now Manitoba; the earth had been washed down from the mountains. That is still going on at the mouth of the Saskatchewan river before it flows into the lakes and if dikes were not put there it would rise up and flood and leave another layer or maybe two or three inches of earth; and in due course over a long period of time they would flood. But the government is stopping the flooding now in order that farmers can go in and work that land.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Suppose a province had a particularly difficult situation on its hands and it sought the assistance of the dominion in dealing with the problem. Does the dominion enter into the picture in a situation like that?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: That is what this vote is for. Where a province makes application and where it is prepared to spend a certain proportion of the amount, we enter into an agreement with it.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Shall the item
carry?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
I understand, Mr. Chairman, this would be the correct item under which to inquire with regard to the special projects in the province of Manitoba which I have discussed on one or two other occasions. I should like to ask the minister at this time if he is in a position to inform the committee as to what specific projects in regard to flood control are being undertaken in the province of Manitoba, more particularly in the northwest portion in the run-off area of Riding mountain and Duck mountain.
I might say that I have inquired on one or two occasions of the minister of agriculture of the province of Manitoba and he has informed me that for one reason or another which I shall not go into now, he would prefer that the information be given by the federal government rather than from his own office. Specifically, I should like to know what projects are being undertaken this year or will be undertaken this year in the area north of Riding mountain and east of Duck mountain.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: I read those a few moments ago; I do not think my hon. friend was in the house at the time. Riding-Duck mountain watershed and Porcupine forest reserve, $150,000; Saskatchewan river reclamation, Pasqua area, $500,000. The other amount that is being allotted is down in Newfoundland.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
It so happens, Mr. Chairman, that I was aware of that. What my question refers to is this. Specifically what is being done with that $150,000? That is information

which I am not able to obtain from the provincial department of agriculture. This therefore seems to be the only place where it can be obtained. As a matter of fact that is the advice I received from the minister of agriculture of Manitoba. He referred me to the federal department on account of the fact that, according to him, these projects must be approved by the federal government before their contribution can be made. I should like to know specifically what is being done with the $150,000 this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
The agreement that is
entered into with the province which results in a dollar for dollar expenditure is made for an amount to cover a certain area. The province determines where that money is going to be spent and they spend it, as a matter of fact, on the works around Dauphin lake on both sides of Riding mountain. That money is spent by the provincial government and they bill us with half the cost. Hence they have more information about it. Until the work is actually going on or until we are billed we have no information; that is we have no final information. We do the engineering, and from that we have some idea as to what they are going to do.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
I am inclined to take the same view as the minister in this regard. That was my understanding also. But may I quote to him a portion of a letter that I received from the minister of agriculture of Manitoba dated July 5, in reply to an inquiry of mine. In that letter he said:
I suggest you inquire from either Mr. Matte in Ottawa or directly from Dr. L. B. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext: If this $150,000 is spent you can get the information from here as to where it is spent, because we will not pay it unless we know where it was spent and how it was spent. I am hardly satisfied with that answer, Mr. Chairman. We have now reached the third day of August. As the minister knows, with the kind of season we

have in western Canada on the prairies, any work that is to be undertaken this year will certainly have to be at least in the blueprint stage by August 3. I strongly suggest that it is not good enough to say that perhaps the province does not know either. I might say that this matter does not concern my own constituency alone. 46.	Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act, $1,920,601.

I just want to say a word with respect to this maritime marshland scheme. This is a project which has been carried on in the maritime provinces for a number of years.
I know that in my own constituency it has already done a tremendous amount of good. You can see a considerable increase in the livestock population. I have every reason to believe that similar circumstances exist in other parts of the province. I hope the work will continue to go forward.
I may say that it seems to me when the engineers first undertook this project they were dealing with something about which they did not know very much. They had not the experience, coming from the west as some of them did, with the tides of the bay of Fundy around which these projects are located. However, they are beginning to become acquainted with the problems and I think the work is now being conducted in a very efficient manner.
In this connection I have before me a resolution which was passed by the Nova Scotia federation of agriculture at its annual meeting at Truro last December. This is resolution No. 2 and reads:
Whereas loss from fresh water erosion continues [DOT] to be a serious problem to farmers throughout the province, and
Whereas there is no provision made to control fresh water erosion as it affects farm land.
Resolved that the federation of agriculture petition the provincial and federal authorities to enact legislation similar to the marshland reclamation act to control fresh water erosion of agricultural land.
My request tonight, Mr. Minister, now that we have a very efficient organization of engineers working on the marshland problem, is that thought should be given to some sort of similar scheme for work on the valleys of our rivers in the maritime provinces where every year, with every flash flood and every freshet in the spring, we are losing a good

many acres of very valuable land. I suppose it could be said that there is a water act under which the federal government will pay 35 per cent and the provinces and municipalities will pay the rest, in order to control floods. I am afraid, however, that there is little chance of any work being done under that act.
We have this engineering staff down there and I know there is a big problem on such rivers as the Salmon, the Shubenacadie, the North, the Stewiacke, the Musqodobit, the Nine Mile and many others. As I say, each year the farmers are losing a lot of their valuable land. I am just asking the minister if he will take under advisement having his engineers, when they are around these other projects, study the nature of these valleys. There are members of the staff there who could develop some workable scheme that would be of immense value to our agriculturists in the maritime provinces.
Perhaps I might also come back to the suggestion of the Prime Minister, that if the Atlantic provinces produce a scheme for their general good the federal government would give serious consideration to it. I am suggesting that possibly this scheme which I have suggested for the benefit of agriculture in those provinces would be a good place to start.

The minister told us a year or two ago that some surveys had been continued to that end, and I am wondering whether there has been any further progress in that direction. I think there may be, Mr. Chairman, because I heard of one or two persons who are buying property along the place where the proposed dam would be erected, and I think possibly they may be a little bit optimistic in thinking the dam will be constructed.
In the not too distant future there will undoubtedly be an opportunity there to save substantial sums of money in the maintenance of those dikes, although actually in the meantime I think the minister under this project has rebuilt quite a few of the dikes. Even so you have, as I say, probably 25 miles of dikes running along each side of the river; and if, as the minister intimated two years ago, the surveys indicated that a dam was feasible, then by building a relatively short dam across the river one could avoid the necessity of maintaining 40 or 50 miles of dikes.
I am bringing this to the attention of the minister now particularly because in a letter I had from an engineer, who is resident in the constituency and near this point, he told me that in his opinion the situation is such that the bridge across that river will require major repairs and probably reconstruction within the next four or five years. It would seem to me that if anything is ever going to be done on this project, it should be done in the relatively immediate future when, by the combination of a bridge and a causeway, the minister could effect cooperation with the provincial government in so far as the department of highways is concerned.

Supply-Agriculture
If you put a bridge across the river it will conserve a tremendous quantity of marshland and also save current expenditures, which will be substantial, on the dikes running up and down the river for many years to come. I would like the minister to tell us what the situation is at the moment.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE

Well, the situation is that it is possible to build the dam across the mouth of the river and to prevent the sea from coming in. It is a combination of two things. The sea comes in, as my hon. friend knows, and creates a sort of greasy mud situation which is not very good to look at and not very useful for any purpose. Therefore in most cases we simply build the dikes and keep the water out. Along the river we have been doing that, at least it has been done in past ages by people who were there, and we have taken it on recently and are considering building the dams up along the river.
The suggestion is that instead of doing that we should build a dam right across the mouth of the river. There is a bridge there which is not in very good repair, and probably would have to be rebuilt. I think the provincial government have estimated that it is going to cost them $1 million to put the bridge in and maintain it. They have said they are prepared to pay $1 million toward the building of the dam, the total cost of which would be something over $3 million, about $3,500,000. Some people argue that the cost is so great, as compared with the amount of farm land that is going to be put into use as a result of having built it, that it is out of all proportion.
There are some who take the position that that is not the right way to look at it. Up to now the discussions have gone on, but no conclusion has yet been arrived at as to whether it will be proceeded with or not.

47.	Prairie Farm Assistance Act administration. $502,137.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister is well aware that there are perennial complaints concerning the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, particularly in the province of Manitoba. When the session began this year we anticipated that some amendments might be made to the act which would have solved some of these difficulties. Unfortunately these amendments have not been brought before us, and I would just like to briefly bring to the attention of the minister once again the major points of complaint concerning the administration of the P.F.R.A.
The problem that reaches me quite regularly is that of crown lands where no assistance is payable in cases of crop failure. The complaint arises because notwithstanding the fact that farmers operating on crown lands are forced to contribute to the P.F.A.A. fund, when they need assistance they are not permitted to receive it under the regulations. I understand that V.L.A. land is the only crown land that is exempted from this particularly discriminatory regulation.
There is also the other problem that has arisen as a result of repeated flooding in the area of the Assiniboine valley. Some of the farmers along the Assiniboine valley have suffered crop failures as frequently as three years in succession, with the result that they have had to seek employment off the land. Unfortunately when they have earned income other than from the operation of their farms they are automatically disqualified from receiving payments under the act. This is a special problem. I do not know whether the special cases could be taken care of by regulation under the act, but it is a problem that occurs frequently enough, especially in Manitoba, to require some attention.
Then, of course, in contemplating any amendments to the act there is the fact that the present rates of payment were established in 1939 with a maximum of $500, I believe, and $2.50 per acre. Those figures are out of touch with reality in terms of today's inflationary conditions. I feel that any amendments contemplated should take into consideration the changes in the value of our money and the effects of increasing inflation, and should be designed to place the scheme in a more equitable position.
In Manitoba we are faced with an additional special problem. It is well known to the minister that we always contribute more to the fund than we are able to withdraw because there is not so much marginal land in the province of Manitoba. As a result of the situation the provincial authorities appointed a commission to consider the possibility of establishing some sort of an insurance scheme.

Supply-Agriculture
That commission reported, and the essence of their report was that it would be impossible to operate a crop insurance program by one province. Any adequate crop insurance coverage would require the co-operation of the three prairie provinces. The report intimated further that any initiative in an attempt to bring the three provinces together to make a more comprehensive insurance scheme would possibly have to come from the federal authorities. I wish the minister would comment on that particular aspect of the commission's report.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, there is the special problem which has also arisen from recurring floods in Manitoba. Some payment was available from the prairie farm assistance fund, but there has been almost universal complaint that the payment of $1.25 per acre has hardly been adequate to meet the disastrous effects of the flood conditions.
If I might be allowed while I am on my feet to deal with a matter out of order, Mr. Chairman, I would like to proceed with it. We have stood item 41, but I think it will save time if I speak about this now. I would like to direct this question to the minister because I think some attempt to deal permanently with flood conditions would be a much better scheme in the long run than attempting to meet the cost of damage resulting from annual flood conditions. This, of course, must be taken up under the prairie farm rehabilitation scheme.
The minister is well aware that farmers in Manitoba have become very active in seeking a solution to this problem of flooding. During the Easter recess I attended a meeting at which the director of the P.F.R.A. spoke, and he made a very excellent presentation and helped to clarify my thinking as to a solution to this problem. He placed the responsibility for initial action squarely on the provincial and municipal authorities, and he was supported in this approach to the problem by the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa. The hon. member conducted a survey of flooding on the Assiniboine when it was at its height during the recent spring condition.

speechtext: I can put my question in the next sentence and that will save a speech on item 41. speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as to the last question I think we had better leave the answer to that until other hon. members have presented their case. In so far as item 47 is concerned, I should like to call attention to one or two things. First, for the first time we have paid out a greater amount in Manitoba than the 1 per cent levy that has been paid in. In 1954-55 the amount collected under the 1 per cent levy in Manitoba was $748,694.05 and the amount paid out was $5,009,814. That is largely due to the fact that the act was amended to cover such conditions as we had in 1954. The 1955 amendments made it possible to pay where it was not drought that caused the damage, and so from now on the Manitoba position will be different from what it has been in the past. I just wanted to say that so hon. members might examine the figures and find what had been paid out.
That does not apply only in Manitoba, it applies to the eastern side of the province of Saskatchewan. Drought is the big problem in the western and southwestern portions of the province, it is not so much a matter of submarginal land. My hon. friend referred to the fact that there was not as much submarginal land in Manitoba as there was in Saskatchewan. In that area I am not too sure about that. The reason we apply this act to a township rather than to individual farms is to eliminate the submarginal land. The fact that there has been a crop of more than 8 bushels to the acre in a whole township prevents a man coming in who has poor land and that is the reason his crop is down rather than the weather. Those are facts which are sometimes forgotten when we are discussing this matter.
Then there was the other question as to the value of the dollar. That was not the main thing taken into consideration when the act was set up. The first thing was that we based it on so much per acre, but the other was based on so much grain produced on the acre. When you take into consideration the price of grain now as compared with the price then and add the two things together, you

find that the amount of money paid now more than takes care of the difference in the value of currency at this time as compared with when the act was set up.
Then the statement was made that some people do not like not being paid when they have land and are engaged in some other line of activity. If a man is actually on a farm, if farming is his main operation, then he comes under the act. He can go to work for a neighbouring farmer or go out threshing, but he still comes under the act for payment. But if a man is carrying on farming but his main occupation is that of a merchant he is not paid.
The whole objective of this legislation was to make it possible in a dry year for the farmer to pay his store bill. When he pays his store bill the storekeeper is presumed to get as great an advantage from the act as does the man who has a store bill to pay. It is not intended that the amount paid will be any more than the average store bill. The act was set up to help not only the farmer but the merchant in the small town. Therefore we say that if a man is a station agent or is running an elevator or is in the business of selling commodities, he is taken care of in other ways than under this act and we do not pay him.
I agree that there have been some complaints in Manitoba as well as in the eastern side of Saskatchewan. The reason is that most of these people have come in for the first time, and we get many complaints from storekeepers and others. But where they have been in since 1939 we find there are not the same number of complaints. We always get complaints when a new district comes in, and until they have had experience with the act we will continue to get them. But after they have been under the act for a few years, as it is now in Manitoba, there are not the same complaints made.

speechtext: What about the farmer in a dry area seeking supplementary employment off the farm when the farm is in a flooded area? A man may have a crop failure and take temporary employment, for example in the oil fields around Virden. This is the area where most of the complaints have originated. They have been denied payment under the act because they have been in receipt of income from other than agricultural activities, but this employment has been temporary in order to meet an emergency.
